name: Firm performance
definition: The overall degree to which a firm attains its economic and strategic goals, encompassing financial results, product-market outcomes, growth and survival. It is the umbrella concept under which more specific performance dimensions are organized.
sign_convention: higher values mean better overall firm performance
citations: Venkatraman, N.; Ramanujam, V. (1986). Measurement of business performance in strategy research: A comparison of approaches. Academy of Management Review; Richard, P. J.; Devinney, T. M.; Yip, G. S.; Johnson, G. (2009). Measuring organizational performance: Towards methodological best practice. Journal of Management
aliases: Organizational performance; Corporate performance; Company performance; Organization performance; Business success; Overall firm performance; Firm success

name: Financial performance
definition: A firm's performance in economic terms as reflected in accounting results and capital-market valuation, the narrowest and most common domain of business performance in strategy research.
sign_convention: higher values mean better financial performance
citations: Venkatraman, N.; Ramanujam, V. (1986). Measurement of business performance in strategy research: A comparison of approaches. Academy of Management Review
aliases: Firm financial performance; Corporate financial performance; Economic performance; Firm economic performance

name: Profitability
definition: The accounting-based return a firm earns on its sales, assets or equity, reflecting the surplus of revenues over costs generated by operations.
sign_convention: higher values mean higher profitability
citations: Venkatraman, N.; Ramanujam, V. (1986). Measurement of business performance in strategy research: A comparison of approaches. Academy of Management Review; Combs, J. G.; Crook, T. R.; Shook, C. L. (2005). The dimensionality of organizational performance and its implications for strategic management research. Research Methodology in Strategy and Management
aliases: Firm profitability; Corporate profitability; Accounting performance; Operating performance; Operating profitability; Accounting returns; Return; Earnings performance

name: Firm growth
definition: The rate at which a firm expands its scale of activity over time, typically in sales, employment or assets.
sign_convention: higher values mean faster growth
citations: Delmar, F.; Davidsson, P.; Gartner, W. B. (2003). Arriving at the high-growth firm. Journal of Business Venturing
aliases: Growth; Organizational growth; Company growth

name: Sales growth
definition: The rate of increase in a firm's sales revenue between periods, the most widely used indicator of firm growth.
sign_convention: higher values mean faster sales growth
citations: Delmar, F.; Davidsson, P.; Gartner, W. B. (2003). Arriving at the high-growth firm. Journal of Business Venturing
aliases: Revenue growth; Growth of sales; Sales growth rate; Relative sales growth

name: Employment growth
definition: The rate of change in the number of people a firm employs.
sign_convention: higher values mean faster employment growth
citations: Delmar, F.; Davidsson, P.; Gartner, W. B. (2003). Arriving at the high-growth firm. Journal of Business Venturing
aliases: Headcount growth; Job growth

name: Market-based performance
definition: A firm's performance as assessed by the capital market, whether as the level of its market valuation, the returns earned by its shareholders, or the market's reaction to firm events.
sign_convention: higher values mean better market-assessed performance
citations: Venkatraman, N.; Ramanujam, V. (1986). Measurement of business performance in strategy research: A comparison of approaches. Academy of Management Review; Richard, P. J.; Devinney, T. M.; Yip, G. S.; Johnson, G. (2009). Measuring organizational performance: Towards methodological best practice. Journal of Management
aliases: Market performance; Stock market performance; Capital market performance; Market-based firm performance

name: Firm value
definition: The capital market's valuation of a firm, reflecting investors' expectations of its future cash flows relative to the resources it employs.
sign_convention: higher values mean a higher market valuation
citations: Chung, K. H.; Pruitt, S. W. (1994). A simple approximation of Tobin's q. Financial Management
aliases: Market valuation; Market value; Shareholder value; Firm valuation; Firm market value; Tobin's q; Market-to-book ratio; Market capitalization

name: Excess value
definition: The difference between a firm's actual market value and the value it would have if each of its business segments were valued as a stand-alone single-segment firm.
sign_convention: higher values mean a valuation premium (a less negative diversification discount)
citations: Berger, P. G.; Ofek, E. (1995). Diversification's effect on firm value. Journal of Financial Economics
aliases: Excess firm value; Diversification premium; Diversification discount (reverse)

name: Shareholder returns
definition: The realized return earned by a firm's shareholders over a holding period, combining share price appreciation and dividends, with or without adjustment for a benchmark.
sign_convention: higher values mean higher returns to shareholders
citations: Richard, P. J.; Devinney, T. M.; Yip, G. S.; Johnson, G. (2009). Measuring organizational performance: Towards methodological best practice. Journal of Management
aliases: Stock returns; Total shareholder return; Stock market returns; Holding period returns; Buy-and-hold abnormal returns; Long-term shareholder return

name: Stock market reaction
definition: The change in a firm's market value attributable to a specific announcement or event, captured as the abnormal stock return over a short event window.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more favorable market reaction
citations: McWilliams, A.; Siegel, D. (1997). Event studies in management research: Theoretical and empirical issues. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Abnormal stock returns; Cumulative abnormal return; Investor reactions; Announcement returns; Stock price reaction; Event study returns; Shareholder wealth effect; Market reaction to CEO appointment; Stock market reaction to CEO appointment; Investor reactions to new CEO appointment; Succession announcement returns

name: Performance change
definition: The change in a firm's performance level from an earlier period to a later one, whether measured as a difference, a growth rate or a deviation from the firm's own past.
sign_convention: higher values mean a larger performance improvement
aliases: Change in firm performance; Performance improvement; Profitability change; Change in profitability; Deviation from prior performance

name: Performance persistence
definition: The degree to which a firm's superior (or abnormal) performance is sustained over time rather than converging toward the norm.
sign_convention: higher values mean performance advantages persist longer
citations: Jacobsen, R. (1988). The persistence of abnormal returns. Strategic Management Journal; Wiggins, R. R.; Ruefli, T. W. (2002). Sustained competitive advantage: Temporal dynamics and the incidence and persistence of superior economic performance. Organization Science
aliases: Profit persistence; Persistent superior economic performance; Sustained superior performance; Persistence of abnormal returns

name: Risk-adjusted performance
definition: A firm's or fund's return expressed per unit of the risk borne to earn it, such as a return scaled by its variability or a return in excess of what its risk exposure would predict.
sign_convention: higher values mean better risk-adjusted performance
aliases: Risk-adjusted return; Sharpe ratio; Alpha; Information ratio

name: Firm survival
definition: The continued existence of a firm as an independent operating organization over time, the complement of failure, exit or dissolution.
sign_convention: higher values mean a greater likelihood or longer duration of survival
citations: Freeman, J.; Carroll, G. R.; Hannan, M. T. (1983). The liability of newness: Age dependence in organizational death rates. American Sociological Review
aliases: Organizational survival; Survival; Firm failure (reverse); Firm mortality (reverse); Organizational mortality (reverse); Business mortality (reverse); Firm exit (reverse); Organizational dissolution (reverse); Exit hazard (reverse); Organizational failure (reverse); Bankruptcy (reverse)

name: Operational performance
definition: A firm's performance on nonfinancial outcomes that lead to financial results, such as market position, productivity, efficiency and quality.
sign_convention: higher values mean better operational performance
citations: Venkatraman, N.; Ramanujam, V. (1986). Measurement of business performance in strategy research: A comparison of approaches. Academy of Management Review
aliases: Operational effectiveness; Nonfinancial performance; Operating outcomes

name: Product market performance
definition: The success of a firm's products or services in the market, reflected in sales volume, customer acceptance and share of the market.
sign_convention: higher values mean greater product-market success
citations: Richard, P. J.; Devinney, T. M.; Yip, G. S.; Johnson, G. (2009). Measuring organizational performance: Towards methodological best practice. Journal of Management
aliases: Market success; Commercial success; Market acceptance

name: Market share
definition: The proportion of total sales or output in a defined market that is captured by the focal firm.
sign_convention: higher values mean a larger share of the market
citations: Buzzell, R. D.; Gale, B. T.; Sultan, R. G. M. (1975). Market share: A key to profitability. Harvard Business Review
aliases: Share of market

name: Sales performance
definition: The level of revenue or unit volume a firm or unit generates from selling its products or services, treated as a top-line performance outcome.
sign_convention: higher values mean higher sales
aliases: Sales; Revenue; Firm revenue; Sales volume; Revenue performance; Unit sales; Product sales

name: Firm productivity
definition: The efficiency with which a firm converts inputs such as labor, capital and materials into output.
sign_convention: higher values mean higher productivity
citations: Syverson, C. (2011). What determines productivity?. Journal of Economic Literature
aliases: Productivity; Output-input ratio; Economic productivity

name: Labor productivity
definition: Output or value added per unit of labor input, indicating how efficiently a firm's workforce creates output.
sign_convention: higher values mean higher output per worker
citations: Datta, D. K.; Guthrie, J. P.; Wright, P. M. (2005). Human resource management and labor productivity: Does industry matter?. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Employee productivity; Labour productivity; Sales per employee; Value added per employee

name: Total factor productivity
definition: The portion of a firm's output not explained by the quantity of its capital, labor and material inputs, reflecting overall production efficiency.
sign_convention: higher values mean higher total factor productivity
citations: Syverson, C. (2011). What determines productivity?. Journal of Economic Literature
aliases: TFP; Multifactor productivity; Plant productivity

name: Operating efficiency
definition: The extent to which a firm or unit produces its output at low cost or with minimal input, whether judged against a best-practice frontier, against peers or through cost and asset-use ratios.
sign_convention: higher values mean greater efficiency (lower cost per unit of output)
aliases: Cost efficiency; Operational efficiency; Productive efficiency; Technical efficiency; Resource efficiency; Manufacturing efficiency

name: Product and service quality
definition: The degree to which a firm's products or services meet customer requirements and performance standards, including reliability and conformance.
sign_convention: higher values mean higher quality
citations: Garvin, D. A. (1987). Competing on the eight dimensions of quality. Harvard Business Review
aliases: Product quality; Service quality; Quality performance; Product reliability

name: Safety performance
definition: The extent to which an organization avoids accidents, injuries and safety incidents in its operations.
sign_convention: higher values mean safer operations (fewer accidents or incidents)
aliases: Safety outcomes; Operational safety; Accident rate (reverse); Accident count (reverse); Adverse safety events; Adverse events; Accidents; Safety incidents

name: Customer performance
definition: The outcomes a firm achieves with its customers, such as retention, loyalty and satisfaction.
sign_convention: higher values mean better customer outcomes
aliases: Customer retention; Customer loyalty outcomes; Customer satisfaction outcomes

name: Business unit performance
definition: The overall performance of a division, strategic business unit, segment, plant or store within a larger firm, assessed on multiple or unspecified dimensions of the unit's own results. A unit's accounting profitability specifically is a variant of Profitability.
sign_convention: higher values mean better unit performance
citations: Dess, G. G.; Robinson, R. B. (1984). Measuring organizational performance in the absence of objective measures: The case of the privately-held firm and conglomerate business unit. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Unit performance; Business performance; SBU performance; SBU effectiveness; Business segment performance; Unit-level performance; Store performance; Plant performance; Establishment performance

name: Subsidiary performance
definition: The performance of a subsidiary or affiliate that is owned and controlled by a parent firm, typically a foreign affiliate of a multinational, assessed on the subsidiary's own results.
sign_convention: higher values mean better subsidiary performance
aliases: Affiliate performance; Foreign subsidiary performance; Foreign affiliate performance; Subsidiary financial performance

name: Fund performance
definition: The investment return generated by a managed investment vehicle such as a mutual fund, hedge fund or venture capital fund for its investors.
sign_convention: higher values mean higher fund returns
aliases: Investment fund returns; Fund returns

name: Acquisition performance
definition: The extent to which an acquisition creates value for the acquiring firm and its shareholders, assessed through market reactions, post-deal accounting results or managerial evaluations.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more successful acquisition
citations: Zollo, M.; Meier, D. (2008). What is M&A performance?. Academy of Management Perspectives; King, D. R.; Dalton, D. R.; Daily, C. M.; Covin, J. G. (2004). Meta-analyses of post-acquisition performance: Indications of unidentified moderators. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: M&A performance; Merger performance; Acquisition success; Acquirer performance; M&A success; Value creation in acquisitions; Acquisition efficiency; Total gains to the combined firm; Synergy realization

name: Acquirer announcement returns
definition: The abnormal stock return earned by the acquiring firm around the announcement of an acquisition, reflecting investors' expectations of the deal's value.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more favorable market reaction to the acquirer
citations: Zollo, M.; Meier, D. (2008). What is M&A performance?. Academy of Management Perspectives
aliases: Acquirer abnormal returns; Bidder announcement returns; Acquisition returns; Market reaction to acquisition announcement

name: Long-term acquisition performance
definition: The performance of the acquiring or combined firm in the years after a deal, measured by post-acquisition accounting results or long-run stock returns.
sign_convention: higher values mean better post-acquisition performance
citations: King, D. R.; Dalton, D. R.; Daily, C. M.; Covin, J. G. (2004). Meta-analyses of post-acquisition performance: Indications of unidentified moderators. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Post-acquisition performance; Postdeal performance; Postacquisition operating performance; Postmerger stock returns; Long-run acquirer returns

name: Performance feedback
definition: The comparison of an organization's realized performance with a reference level such as its aspiration or external expectations, which signals whether performance is satisfactory and triggers search and change.
sign_convention: higher values mean performance further above the reference level
citations: Cyert, R. M.; March, J. G. (1963). A Behavioral Theory of the Firm. Prentice-Hall (book); Greve, H. R. (2003). Organizational Learning from Performance Feedback: A Behavioral Perspective on Innovation and Change. Cambridge University Press (book)
aliases: Performance relative to reference point; Performance deviation

name: Performance relative to aspirations
definition: The signed difference between a firm's performance and its aspiration level, whether the aspiration is derived from the firm's own history or from the performance of comparable organizations.
sign_convention: higher values mean performance further above the aspiration level
citations: Greve, H. R. (1998). Performance, aspirations, and risky organizational change. Administrative Science Quarterly
aliases: Attainment discrepancy; Aspiration gap; Aspiration-performance gap; Performance relative to aspiration level; Social aspiration performance; Historical aspiration performance

name: Performance above aspirations
definition: The extent to which a firm's performance exceeds its aspiration level, set to zero when performance falls short, as used in spline specifications of performance feedback.
sign_convention: higher values mean performance exceeds aspirations by more
citations: Greve, H. R. (1998). Performance, aspirations, and risky organizational change. Administrative Science Quarterly
aliases: Positive attainment discrepancy; Performance surplus; Positive performance feedback

name: Performance below aspirations
definition: The extent to which a firm's performance falls short of its aspiration level, set to zero when performance meets or exceeds aspirations, as used in spline specifications of performance feedback.
sign_convention: higher values mean a larger shortfall of performance below the aspiration level
citations: Greve, H. R. (1998). Performance, aspirations, and risky organizational change. Administrative Science Quarterly
aliases: Negative attainment discrepancy; Performance shortfall; Negative performance feedback; Negative performance gap

name: Earnings surprise
definition: The difference between a firm's reported earnings and the consensus earnings forecast of securities analysts for the same period.
sign_convention: higher values mean reported earnings exceed analyst forecasts by more
aliases: Performance relative to analyst forecasts; Analyst forecast error; Earnings relative to consensus forecasts

name: Negative earnings surprise
definition: The extent to which reported earnings fall below analysts' consensus forecast, set to zero when the forecast is met or beaten.
sign_convention: higher values mean a larger shortfall below analyst forecasts
aliases: Earnings miss; Missing analyst forecasts

name: Analyst earnings expectations
definition: The level of earnings that securities analysts, on consensus, forecast a firm will report, serving as the reference point against which earnings surprises are judged.
sign_convention: higher values mean higher expected earnings
aliases: Analysts' EPS expectations; Consensus earnings forecast; Performance expectations

name: Earnings pressure
definition: The pressure on a firm to meet or beat securities analysts' earnings forecasts, arising when forecasts exceed the earnings the firm can generate under its current course.
sign_convention: higher values mean greater pressure to meet earnings expectations
citations: Zhang, Y.; Gimeno, J. (2010). Earnings pressure and competitive behavior: Evidence from the U.S. electricity industry. Administrative Science Quarterly
aliases: Pressure to meet analyst forecasts

name: Firm risk
definition: The uncertainty or variability of a firm's performance outcomes, whether observed in its stock returns, its income stream or the likelihood of falling below a target.
sign_convention: higher values mean greater risk
citations: Miller, K. D.; Bromiley, P. (1990). Strategic risk and corporate performance: An analysis of alternative risk measures. Academy of Management Journal; Ruefli, T. W.; Collins, J. M.; Lacugna, J. R. (1999). Risk measures in strategic management research: Auld lang syne?. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Organizational risk; Business risk; Total risk; Corporate risk; Risk

name: Stock return volatility
definition: The variability of a firm's stock returns over time, the capital-market view of total firm risk.
sign_convention: higher values mean more volatile stock returns
citations: Miller, K. D.; Bromiley, P. (1990). Strategic risk and corporate performance: An analysis of alternative risk measures. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Variance of returns; Stock price volatility; Total stock risk; Market-based risk; Firm stock risk

name: Systematic risk
definition: The component of a firm's stock return variability that moves with the market as a whole, captured by the firm's beta.
sign_convention: higher values mean greater systematic risk
citations: Lubatkin, M.; Chatterjee, S. (1994). Extending modern portfolio theory into the domain of corporate diversification: Does it apply?. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Beta; Market risk; Stockholder risk

name: Unsystematic risk
definition: The component of a firm's stock return variability that is specific to the firm and not explained by market-wide movements.
sign_convention: higher values mean greater firm-specific risk
citations: Lubatkin, M.; Chatterjee, S. (1994). Extending modern portfolio theory into the domain of corporate diversification: Does it apply?. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Idiosyncratic risk; Idiosyncratic volatility; Firm-specific risk; Residual risk

name: Income stream risk
definition: The variability or ex ante uncertainty of a firm's accounting earnings over time.
sign_convention: higher values mean more variable earnings
citations: Bromiley, P. (1991). Testing a causal model of corporate risk taking and performance. Academy of Management Journal; Miller, K. D.; Bromiley, P. (1990). Strategic risk and corporate performance: An analysis of alternative risk measures. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Earnings risk; Earnings volatility; Profit volatility; Performance variability; Income stream uncertainty; Accounting risk

name: Downside risk
definition: The probability-weighted extent to which a firm's performance falls below a target level, capturing only unfavorable outcomes rather than variability in both directions.
sign_convention: higher values mean greater downside risk
citations: Miller, K. D.; Leiblein, M. J. (1996). Corporate risk-return relations: Returns variability versus downside risk. Academy of Management Journal; Reuer, J. J.; Leiblein, M. J. (2000). Downside risk implications of multinationality and international joint ventures. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Lower partial moment; Below-target risk

name: Financial condition
definition: The overall financial health of a firm, reflecting its liquidity, cash generation, indebtedness and distance from insolvency.
sign_convention: higher values mean a healthier financial condition
aliases: Financial health; Financial status; Firm financial condition; Financial strength

name: Liquidity
definition: The extent to which a firm holds cash and other assets that can readily meet its short-term obligations.
sign_convention: higher values mean greater liquidity
aliases: Firm liquidity; Current ratio; Asset liquidity; Liquidity; Cash holdings

name: Cash flow
definition: The funds a firm generates from its operations in a period, indicating its capacity to finance investment internally.
sign_convention: higher values mean larger cash flow
aliases: Operating cash flow; Internal funds

name: Free cash flow
definition: Cash flow in excess of what is required to fund all projects with positive net present value, which managers may retain or distribute.
sign_convention: higher values mean more free cash flow
citations: Jensen, M. C. (1986). Agency costs of free cash flow, corporate finance, and takeovers. American Economic Review
aliases: FCF; Excess cash flow

name: Financial distress
definition: The degree to which a firm is at risk of being unable to meet its financial obligations, ranging from cash-flow strain to imminent bankruptcy.
sign_convention: higher values mean greater financial distress (closer to bankruptcy)
citations: Altman, E. I. (1968). Financial ratios, discriminant analysis and the prediction of corporate bankruptcy. Journal of Finance
aliases: Bankruptcy risk; Default risk; Proximity to bankruptcy; Distance from bankruptcy (reverse); Financial distress risk

name: Cost of capital
definition: The return a firm must offer its providers of debt and equity capital, which sets the discount rate applied to its investments.
sign_convention: higher values mean costlier capital
aliases: Weighted average cost of capital; Discount rate

name: Cost of equity capital
definition: The return required by a firm's shareholders, typically estimated from the firm's systematic risk or realized long-run returns.
sign_convention: higher values mean a higher required return on equity
aliases: Cost of equity; Required return on equity

name: Dividend payout
definition: The extent to which a firm distributes earnings to shareholders as dividends rather than retaining them.
sign_convention: higher values mean larger dividend distributions
aliases: Dividend yield; Payout ratio; Dividend policy

name: Performance heterogeneity
definition: The dispersion and shape of the distribution of performance across organizations or units, and the decomposition of that dispersion into sources such as industry, corporate parent and firm.
sign_convention: higher values mean greater dispersion of performance across units
citations: Rumelt, R. P. (1991). How much does industry matter?. Strategic Management Journal; McGahan, A. M.; Porter, M. E. (1997). How much does industry matter, really?. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Interfirm performance heterogeneity; Performance variance decomposition; Distribution of organizational performance; Intra-industry variance in performance

name: Firm effect
definition: The share of variance in performance across business units or firms that is attributable to stable differences among firms rather than industries, years or corporate parents.
sign_convention: higher values mean a larger share of performance variance attributable to the firm
citations: Rumelt, R. P. (1991). How much does industry matter?. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Firm effects; Business unit effect; Firm-specific variance component

name: Corporate effect
definition: The share of variance in business unit or subsidiary performance that is attributable to differences among corporate parents.
sign_convention: higher values mean a larger share of performance variance attributable to the corporate parent
citations: Bowman, E. H.; Helfat, C. E. (2001). Does corporate strategy matter?. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Corporate parent effect; Corporate-parent effects

name: Performance dispersion
definition: The cross-sectional variance of performance outcomes across the products, units or organizations in a population, as distinct from one unit's variability over time.
sign_convention: higher values mean more dispersed outcomes
aliases: Performance variance; Outcome variance; Variance of outcomes

name: Performance skewness
definition: The asymmetry of the distribution of performance outcomes across units, with positive skew indicating a long tail of exceptional performers.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more positively skewed performance distribution
aliases: Performance distribution skewness

name: Capacity utilization
definition: The proportion of a firm's or unit's available productive capacity that is actually used to produce output.
sign_convention: higher values mean fuller use of capacity
aliases: Occupancy rate; Utilization rate; Output relative to capacity

name: Industry effect
definition: The share of variance in performance across firms or business units that is attributable to the industry in which they operate rather than to the firm, the corporate parent or the year.
sign_convention: higher values mean a larger share of performance variance attributable to industry membership
citations: Rumelt, R. P. (1991). How much does industry matter? Strategic Management Journal, 12(3), 167-185.; McGahan, A. M., & Porter, M. E. (1997). How much does industry matter, really? Strategic Management Journal, 18(S1), 15-30.
aliases: Industry effects; Industry variance component; Industry membership effect

name: Innovation
definition: The generation, development and introduction of new products, processes, technologies or practices by an organization or its members. Umbrella for innovation as an activity and as an outcome.
sign_convention: higher values mean more innovation
citations: Damanpour, F. (1991). Organizational innovation: A meta-analysis of effects of determinants and moderators. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Organizational innovation; Innovations; Technological innovation; Innovative activity

name: Innovation performance
definition: The volume and value of the innovative output an organization produces over a period, such as patented inventions or new products. Typically captured by patent counts, citation-weighted patents or new product output.
sign_convention: higher values mean more and better innovative output
citations: Trajtenberg, M. (1990). A penny for your quotes: Patent citations and the value of innovations. RAND Journal of Economics
aliases: Innovation output; Innovative output; Firm innovation; Firm innovation performance; Corporate innovation; Inventive performance; Innovation outcomes; Technological performance

name: Innovation quantity
definition: The number of innovations or inventions an organization produces in a period, irrespective of their importance.
sign_convention: higher values mean more innovations produced
aliases: Patent output; Patenting output; Patent production; Rate of innovation; Invention quantity; Quantity of innovation; Patent count

name: Innovation quality
definition: The technological importance, impact or economic value of the innovations an organization produces, typically inferred from the forward citations or market value of its patents.
sign_convention: higher values mean more valuable or influential innovations
citations: Trajtenberg, M. (1990). A penny for your quotes: Patent citations and the value of innovations. RAND Journal of Economics; Hall, B. H.; Jaffe, A.; Trajtenberg, M. (2005). Market value and patent citations. RAND Journal of Economics
aliases: Technological impact; Patent value; Knowledge quality; Patent quality; Citation-weighted patents; Innovation value

name: Innovative productivity
definition: The rate at which an organization converts innovation inputs such as R&D spending or researcher effort into innovative output.
sign_convention: higher values mean more innovations per unit of input
aliases: R&D productivity; Research productivity of R&D; Innovation efficiency

name: New product introduction
definition: The number or rate of new products an organization brings to market in a period.
sign_convention: higher values mean more new products introduced
citations: Katila, R.; Ahuja, G. (2002). Something old, something new: A longitudinal study of search behavior and new product introduction. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: New product introductions; Product introduction; Product introductions; Product innovation rate; New product introduction rate; Rate of new product introduction

name: Firm innovativeness
definition: An organization's propensity and capacity to introduce new products, processes and ideas, understood as a general orientation toward novelty rather than a count of any one output.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more innovative firm
citations: Hult, G. T. M.; Hurley, R. F.; Knight, G. A. (2004). Innovativeness: Its antecedents and impact on business performance. Industrial Marketing Management
aliases: Innovativeness; Innovative propensity; Innovative capability; Innovation capability

name: Innovation novelty
definition: The degree to which an organization's innovations depart from existing products, technologies and practices, ranging from incremental improvement to radical departure.
sign_convention: higher values mean more novel or radical innovations
aliases: Novelty of innovation; Innovation radicalness; Innovation radicality; Degree of novelty; New product innovativeness

name: Product innovation
definition: The development and introduction of new or significantly improved goods or services.
sign_convention: higher values mean more product innovation
citations: Damanpour, F. (1991). Organizational innovation: A meta-analysis of effects of determinants and moderators. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Product innovations; Product-related innovation

name: Process innovation
definition: The introduction of new or significantly improved methods of production, delivery or operation.
sign_convention: higher values mean more process innovation
citations: Damanpour, F. (1991). Organizational innovation: A meta-analysis of effects of determinants and moderators. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Process innovations; Process innovation activity; Technical process innovation

name: Radical innovation
definition: Innovation that embodies technology or knowledge entirely new to the firm and its industry, rendering existing technologies obsolete and departing sharply from existing practice.
sign_convention: higher values mean more radical innovation
citations: Henderson, R. M.; Clark, K. B. (1990). Architectural innovation: The reconfiguration of existing product technologies and the failure of established firms. Administrative Science Quarterly
aliases: Drastic innovation; Discontinuous innovation; Novel drug innovation

name: Incremental innovation
definition: Innovation that refines, extends or modifies existing technologies, products or practices within the established technological regime.
sign_convention: higher values mean more incremental innovation
citations: Henderson, R. M.; Clark, K. B. (1990). Architectural innovation: The reconfiguration of existing product technologies and the failure of established firms. Administrative Science Quarterly
aliases: Incremental innovations; Evolutionary innovation; Nondrastic innovation

name: Breakthrough innovation
definition: Inventions of exceptional technological impact, identified as those in the top tail of the citation distribution or as path-breaking departures that open new technological trajectories.
sign_convention: higher values mean more breakthrough inventions
citations: Ahuja, G.; Lampert, C. M. (2001). Entrepreneurship in the large corporation: A longitudinal study of how established firms create breakthrough inventions. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Breakthrough invention; Breakthrough inventions; Path-breaking inventions; Important inventions

name: Exploratory innovation
definition: Innovation that departs from the firm's existing knowledge base to serve new customers, markets or technologies.
sign_convention: higher values mean more exploratory innovation
citations: Jansen, J. J. P.; Van den Bosch, F. A. J.; Volberda, H. W. (2006). Exploratory innovation, exploitative innovation, and performance: Effects of organizational antecedents and environmental moderators. Management Science
aliases: Explorative innovation; Explorative patents

name: Exploitative innovation
definition: Innovation that builds on and refines the firm's own existing knowledge, products and customer markets, defined relative to what the firm already knows. Innovation classified by the small size of its technological change relative to the established technological regime is Incremental innovation.
sign_convention: higher values mean more exploitative innovation
citations: Jansen, J. J. P.; Van den Bosch, F. A. J.; Volberda, H. W. (2006). Exploratory innovation, exploitative innovation, and performance: Effects of organizational antecedents and environmental moderators. Management Science
aliases: Consolidating innovation; Exploitative product innovation

name: Architectural innovation
definition: Innovation that changes the way components of a product are linked together while leaving the core design concepts of the components largely unchanged.
sign_convention: higher values mean more architectural innovation
citations: Henderson, R. M.; Clark, K. B. (1990). Architectural innovation: The reconfiguration of existing product technologies and the failure of established firms. Administrative Science Quarterly

name: Component innovation
definition: Innovation that changes the core design concept of one or more components of a product while leaving the product architecture intact.
sign_convention: higher values mean more component innovation
citations: Henderson, R. M.; Clark, K. B. (1990). Architectural innovation: The reconfiguration of existing product technologies and the failure of established firms. Administrative Science Quarterly

definition: The degree to which the products of two firms resemble or substitute for each other, indicating how directly the firms compete.
sign_convention: higher values mean more similar products
aliases: Interproduct similarity; Product-to-product similarity; Product substitutability; Substitutability

name: Repositioning
definition: A firm's abandonment of its current positioning in product or customer space in favor of a new one.
sign_convention: higher values mean more or larger repositioning
aliases: Strategic repositioning; Market position reconfiguration

name: Multihoming
definition: A complementor's choice to offer its products or services on multiple platforms rather than exclusively on one.
sign_convention: higher values mean presence on more platforms (multihoming rather than singlehoming)
citations: Rochet, J.-C.; Tirole, J. (2003). Platform competition in two-sided markets. Journal of the European Economic Association
aliases: Complement multi-homing

name: Product line breadth
definition: The number of distinct products, variants or services a firm offers in its market, reflecting the breadth of its competitive scope.
sign_convention: higher values mean a broader product line
aliases: Product variety; Product line length; Product range; Number of products; Service offerings; Relative product breadth; Product line breadth

name: Product proliferation
definition: A firm's expansion of the number of products it offers, either within its existing niche or across submarkets, to capture variety-seeking demand and crowd out rivals.
sign_convention: higher values mean more product proliferation
citations: Schmalensee, R. (1978). Entry deterrence in the ready-to-eat breakfast cereal industry. Bell Journal of Economics
aliases: Product line extension

name: Within-niche proliferation
definition: Proliferation that increases the number of products a firm offers within its own niche or submarket.
sign_convention: higher values mean more products within the firm's niche
citations: Barroso, A.; Giarratana, M. S. (2013). Product proliferation strategies and firm performance: The moderating role of product space complexity. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Within-niche product proliferation

name: Across-niche proliferation
definition: Proliferation that extends a firm's offerings into different submarkets or niches.
sign_convention: higher values mean offerings dispersed across more niches
citations: Barroso, A.; Giarratana, M. S. (2013). Product proliferation strategies and firm performance: The moderating role of product space complexity. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Across-niche product proliferation

name: Competitive position
definition: A firm's realized standing in its market relative to rivals, in terms of share, leadership, quality, price, cost and power.
sign_convention: higher values mean a stronger position relative to rivals
aliases: Market position; Relative competitive position; Market standing; Initial competitive position

name: Competitive advantage
definition: The degree to which a firm creates more value relative to its costs than rivals, and hence outperforms them, through a strategy that competitors are not simultaneously implementing.
sign_convention: higher values mean greater competitive advantage
citations: Barney, J. B. (1991). Firm resources and sustained competitive advantage. Journal of Management
aliases: Competitive advantages; Sustained competitive advantage

name: Relative market share
definition: A firm's or product's market share compared with that of its leading competitors or the industry average, including leadership of the market.
sign_convention: higher values mean a larger share relative to rivals
aliases: Market share position; Market leadership; Market share leader; Relative share; Share position; Relative market share

name: Relative product quality
definition: The quality of a business's products or services as perceived by customers compared with the quality offered by its competitors.
sign_convention: higher values mean higher quality relative to competitors
aliases: Relative quality; Product quality relative to competitors

name: Relative price
definition: The price a business charges compared with the prices of its competitors for comparable offerings, including the premium it can command over matched rivals.
sign_convention: higher values mean higher prices relative to competitors
aliases: Relative prices; Price premium; Price relative to competitors

name: Relative cost position
definition: A business's cost level compared with that of its leading competitors, reflecting its realized standing on cost efficiency.
sign_convention: higher values mean a lower cost position than competitors (a cost advantage)
aliases: Cost position; Cost advantage

name: Economies of scale
definition: The improvement in a firm's efficiency or unit cost as its scale of operation increases.
sign_convention: higher values mean stronger scale economies
aliases: Scale economies; Scale efficiency

name: Market power
definition: A firm's ability to set prices above competitive levels in the markets it serves, arising from its share and the concentration of those markets.
sign_convention: higher values mean more market power
aliases: Lerner index; Firm market power

name: Pricing
definition: The price level a firm sets for its offerings and the pricing policy through which it does so.
sign_convention: higher values mean higher prices
aliases: Price; Product price; Price level; Pricing strategy; Room price; Market price

name: Price dispersion
definition: The variability of prices paid for the same or homogeneous products across sellers, buyers or transactions.
sign_convention: higher values mean more dispersed prices
aliases: Price variability; Price variance

name: Freemium strategy
definition: A pricing model in which basic features of a product or service are offered free and customers pay for upgrades to premium features.
sign_convention: higher values mean use of a freemium model
aliases: Freemium business model; Freemium revenue approach; Freemium

name: Market entry and exit
definition: The movement of firms into and out of product or geographic markets, including individual entry and exit events, their timing and mode, aggregate entry and exit rates, and the threat of entry.
sign_convention: categorical umbrella; no ordering, use the children
aliases: Entry and exit; Market entry dynamics

name: Market entry
definition: A firm's move into a product, geographic or service market it did not previously serve.
sign_convention: higher values mean entry occurs or more entries
aliases: Entry; Entry into new markets; Firm market entry; New market entry; Market entry event; Scope expansion; Diversifying entry; Diversification entry; New industry entry; Market expansion; Business scope expansion; Entry into new businesses

name: Product market entry
definition: A firm's entry into a new product category or segment by introducing offerings there for the first time.
sign_convention: higher values mean entry into more or new product categories
aliases: Entry into a product category; Entry into a new product segment; New product category entry

name: Platform owner entry
definition: Entry by a platform owner into the product spaces of its own complementors with first-party offerings.
sign_convention: higher values mean the platform owner enters the complementor's space
citations: Zhu, F.; Liu, Q. (2018). Competing with complementors: An empirical look at Amazon.com. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Platform entry into complementor space; First-party entry

name: Entry timing
definition: How early a firm enters a market relative to other entrants, from first-mover pioneering through early following to late entry.
sign_convention: higher values mean earlier entry (pioneers high, late entrants low)
citations: Lieberman, M. B.; Montgomery, D. B. (1988). First-mover advantages. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Earliness of entry; Timing of market entry; Market pioneering; First-mover status

name: Entry mode
definition: The organizational form through which a firm enters a market, such as internal development, acquisition, joint venture, or de novo versus de alio entry.
sign_convention: categorical; no ordering
aliases: Mode of entry; Diversification mode; Mode of expansion; Diversification entry mode; Acquisition versus greenfield; Internal versus external growth

name: Market exit
definition: A firm's withdrawal from a product, geographic or category market it previously served, while the firm itself continues.
sign_convention: higher values mean exit occurs or more exits
aliases: Market category exit; Exit from a market; Segment exit; Product withdrawal; Line of business exit; Business exit; Exit

name: Product exit
definition: The withdrawal of a specific product or model from the market by the firm that offers it.
sign_convention: higher values mean the product is withdrawn
aliases: Product withdrawal; Product discontinuation

name: Entry rate
definition: The number or rate of firms, including diversifying entrants from other markets, entering a market in a period, including entry in excess of what the market can accommodate. The number of newly founded organizations in a population is New firm founding rate.
sign_convention: higher values mean more entrants
aliases: Number of entrants; Firm entry; Excess entry; Entry density

name: Exit rate
definition: The number or rate of firms exiting a market in a period.
sign_convention: higher values mean more exits
aliases: Incumbent exit; Number of exits; Exit density

name: Market overlap
definition: The extent to which two firms operate in the same product, geographic or customer markets, and hence are direct competitors.
sign_convention: higher values mean more overlap
citations: Chen, M.-J. (1996). Competitor analysis and interfirm rivalry: Toward a theoretical integration. Academy of Management Review
aliases: Product market overlap; Product-market overlap; Market commonality; Competitive overlap; Partner market overlap; Market similarity; Competitor colocation

name: Multimarket contact
definition: The degree to which two actors meet each other as competitors across multiple domains, such as two firms across markets or two securities analysts across the stocks they both cover. Such contact can create conditions for mutual forbearance but does not guarantee it.
sign_convention: higher values mean more multimarket contact
citations: Gimeno, J.; Woo, C. Y. (1996). Hypercompetition in a multimarket environment: The role of strategic similarity and multimarket contact in competitive de-escalation. Organization Science
aliases: Multipoint contact; Multimarket competition; Multimarket contact between partners; MMC

name: Reciprocal multimarket contact
definition: Multimarket contact in which each firm dominates some of the shared markets, so that dominance is reciprocated across markets.
sign_convention: higher values mean more reciprocal multimarket contacts
citations: Gimeno, J. (1999). Reciprocal threats in multimarket rivalry: Staking out 'spheres of influence' in the U.S. airline industry. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Reciprocity of multimarket contacts; Reciprocal multimarket contacts; Reciprocity of market contacts

name: Strategic groups
definition: The intraindustry structure formed by subsets of firms that follow similar strategies and are separated from other subsets by mobility barriers.
sign_convention: categorical umbrella; no ordering, use the children
citations: Caves, R. E.; Porter, M. E. (1977). From entry barriers to mobility barriers: Conjectural decisions and contrived deterrence to new competition. Quarterly Journal of Economics
aliases: Strategic group structure; Intraindustry structure

name: Strategic group membership
definition: The strategic group within its industry to which a firm belongs, as identified from similarity in its strategic posture to other firms.
sign_convention: categorical; no ordering
aliases: Strategic group; Group membership; Strategic group affiliation

name: Mobility barriers
definition: Structural and strategic factors that impede firms from moving between strategic groups within an industry.
sign_convention: higher values mean higher barriers to movement between groups
citations: Caves, R. E.; Porter, M. E. (1977). From entry barriers to mobility barriers: Conjectural decisions and contrived deterrence to new competition. Quarterly Journal of Economics
aliases: Barriers to mobility

name: Rivalry
definition: A competitive relationship between two actors in which the focal actor experiences heightened psychological stakes and involvement when competing against the specific other, beyond what objective competition implies.
sign_convention: higher values mean stronger rivalry toward the specific competitor
citations: Kilduff, G. J.; Elfenbein, H. A.; Staw, B. M. (2010). The psychology of rivalry: A relationally dependent analysis of competition. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Interfirm rivalry; Relational rivalry; Asymmetric rivalry; Interpersonal rivalry

name: Customer switching costs
definition: The costs a customer incurs when changing from one supplier to another, which lock customers in and shield incumbents from competition.
sign_convention: higher values mean higher switching costs for customers
citations: Klemperer, P. (1987). Markets with consumer switching costs. Quarterly Journal of Economics
aliases: Switching costs; Customer lock-in

name: Analysis orientation
definition: The extent to which a firm's strategic posture emphasizes careful analysis, systematic search and comprehensive evaluation of problems and opportunities before acting, combining elements of defending an existing domain and prospecting for new ones. The analyzer type in the Miles and Snow typology and the analysis dimension of the STROBE scale.
sign_convention: higher values mean a stronger analysis (analyzer) orientation
citations: Venkatraman, N. (1989). Strategic orientation of business enterprises: The construct, dimensionality, and measurement. Management Science; Miles, R. E., and Snow, C. C. (1978). Organizational Strategy, Structure, and Process. McGraw-Hill (book)
aliases: Analyzer orientation; Analysis strategic orientation; Analyzer strategic type; Analyzer; STROBE analysis

name: Platform user base
definition: The size and activity of the user side of a multisided platform, reflecting how many users have adopted the platform and how intensively they use it; the installed base that generates the platform's network effects.
sign_convention: higher values mean a larger or more active user base
aliases: Platform usage; Installed base; Platform installed base; Platform traffic; Number of platform users; User engagement on the platform

name: Internationalization
definition: The process and resulting state of a firm's involvement in operations outside its home country, both inward and outward. Umbrella for forms of international involvement and for changes in it over time; the extent to which a firm's activities, sales or assets are spread abroad is International diversification.
sign_convention: higher values mean greater international involvement
citations: Welch, L.S.; Luostarinen, R. (1988). Internationalization: Evolution of a concept. Journal of General Management
aliases: Firm internationalization; International involvement

name: International diversification
definition: The extent to which a firm's activities, sales or assets are spread across countries outside its home market. Covers both the depth of foreign involvement (share of foreign sales, assets or employees) and its breadth (number of countries or regions).
sign_convention: higher values mean a larger share of activity abroad and dispersion across more countries
citations: Hitt, M.A.; Hoskisson, R.E.; Kim, H. (1997). International diversification: Effects on innovation and firm performance in product-diversified firms. Academy of Management Journal; Sullivan, D. (1994). Measuring the degree of internationalization of a firm. Journal of International Business Studies
aliases: Degree of internationalization; Multinationality; Geographic diversification; International diversity; Global market diversification; Foreign sales intensity; Multinational diversity

name: Export intensity
definition: The share of a firm's total sales that is generated by exports from the home country, reflecting reliance on exporting as the channel of serving foreign markets.
sign_convention: higher values mean a larger share of sales exported
aliases: Export ratio; Foreign sales intensity via exports

name: Export performance
definition: The level of a firm's export sales, treated as an outcome of the firm's foreign market activity rather than as a ratio to total sales.
sign_convention: higher values mean more export sales
aliases: Export sales

name: International expansion
definition: The increase over time in a firm's presence outside its home country, through new foreign entries, added countries or growth in foreign sales. Includes the pace at which such expansion occurs.
sign_convention: higher values mean a larger or faster increase in international presence
citations: Vermeulen, F.; Barkema, H. (2002). Pace, rhythm, and scope: Process and product of international expansion. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Internationalising; International diversification growth; Rate of foreign expansion; Speed of international expansion

name: Foreign direct investment
definition: A firm's establishment or acquisition of a wholly or partly owned operating facility or subsidiary in a foreign country, as opposed to investing domestically or serving the market by exports.
sign_convention: higher values mean more (or a higher likelihood of) direct investment abroad
aliases: FDI; International investment; Foreign subsidiary investment

name: Foreign market entry
definition: The event of a firm entering a host country in which it did not previously operate, typically by setting up or acquiring a local affiliate.
sign_convention: higher values mean more (or a higher likelihood of) entry into a foreign market
aliases: Foreign entry; Host country entry

name: Cross-border acquisition
definition: An acquisition in which the acquirer and the target are headquartered in different countries.
sign_convention: higher values mean the acquisition is (or the firm engages more in) cross-border rather than domestic acquisitions
aliases: International acquisition; Cross-border combination; Foreign acquirer

name: Foreign entry mode
definition: The organizational form through which a firm enters a foreign market, ranging from nonequity arrangements to shared-equity joint ventures and wholly owned subsidiaries, and reflecting the degree of ownership control and resource commitment.
sign_convention: higher values mean higher-control, higher-commitment modes (wholly owned rather than joint venture, equity rather than nonequity)
citations: Anderson, E.; Gatignon, H. (1986). Modes of foreign entry: A transaction cost analysis and propositions. Journal of International Business Studies; Kogut, B.; Singh, H. (1988). The effect of national culture on the choice of entry mode. Journal of International Business Studies
aliases: Entry mode choice; Mode of market entry; Foreign subsidiary ownership mode; Ownership mode

name: International joint venture
definition: An equity entry mode in which a foreign entrant shares ownership of the local affiliate with one or more partners, typically a host country firm.
sign_convention: higher values mean the affiliate is (or is preferred to be) a joint venture rather than a wholly owned subsidiary
citations: Hennart, J.-F. (1991). The transaction costs theory of joint ventures: An empirical study of Japanese subsidiaries in the United States. Management Science
aliases: Joint venture entry; IJV; Joint venture status; IJV attractiveness

name: Establishment mode
definition: Whether a foreign affiliate is established by acquiring an existing local firm or by building a new (greenfield) operation.
sign_convention: higher values mean entry by acquisition rather than greenfield
citations: Hennart, J.-F.; Park, Y.-R. (1993). Greenfield vs. acquisition: The strategy of Japanese investors in the United States. Management Science
aliases: Acquisition versus greenfield; Entry through acquisition; Likelihood of acquisition; Propensity to enter by acquisition

name: Foreign affiliate equity ownership
definition: The percentage of equity in a foreign affiliate held by the investing parent, representing a continuous span of ownership control from minority stake to full ownership.
sign_convention: higher values mean a larger parent equity stake in the foreign affiliate
citations: Gomes-Casseres, B. (1989). Ownership structures of foreign subsidiaries: Theory and evidence. Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
aliases: Equity level; Equity share; Equity stake in foreign affiliates; Foreign ownership stake; Extent of control

name: FDI motives
definition: The strategic motivations behind a firm's foreign investment, classically market seeking, resource seeking, efficiency seeking and strategic asset seeking.
sign_convention: higher values mean the investment is more strongly driven by the named motive
citations: Dunning, J.H. (1998). Location and the multinational enterprise: A neglected factor?. Journal of International Business Studies
aliases: Investment motivations; FDI motivation

name: Market-seeking motive
definition: A foreign investment motivation aimed at serving the host market through local production and distribution, often where host market growth exceeds home market growth.
sign_convention: higher values mean a stronger market-seeking motive
citations: Dunning, J.H. (1998). Location and the multinational enterprise: A neglected factor?. Journal of International Business Studies
aliases: Market seeking

name: Resource-seeking motive
definition: A foreign investment motivation driven by the need to access resources that are unavailable or more costly in the home country.
sign_convention: higher values mean a stronger resource-seeking motive
citations: Dunning, J.H. (1998). Location and the multinational enterprise: A neglected factor?. Journal of International Business Studies
aliases: Resource seeking

name: Location choice
definition: A firm's selection of a geographic location (country, region or locality) for a new investment or establishment from among a set of alternative locations.
sign_convention: higher values mean the focal location is (more likely to be) chosen
citations: Alcácer, J.; Chung, W. (2007). Location strategies and knowledge spillovers. Management Science
aliases: FDI location choice; Foreign location choice; MNE location choice; International investment location choice

name: Location factors
definition: Characteristics of a host location that attract or deter investment by outside firms, such as trade barriers, market size, costs, institutions and the prior presence of related firms.
sign_convention: higher values mean the location factor is more pronounced
aliases: Host location characteristics; Location advantages

name: Trade barriers
definition: Tariff and nontariff restrictions on importing into a host country, which raise the cost of serving that market by exports and can be bypassed by producing locally.
sign_convention: higher values mean higher barriers to importing into the host country
aliases: Tariffs; Import barriers

name: Distance
definition: The separation between two actors or locations along a dimension such as geography, culture, institutions or time zone, which raises the cost of coordinating and exchanging across the pair.
sign_convention: higher values mean greater separation
citations: Ghemawat, P. (2001). Distance still matters: The hard reality of global expansion. Harvard Business Review
aliases: Home-host country distance; Cross-national distance

name: Cultural distance
definition: The degree to which the national cultures of two countries, typically a firm's home country and a host country, differ in shared values and norms.
sign_convention: higher values mean larger differences between the two national cultures
citations: Kogut, B.; Singh, H. (1988). The effect of national culture on the choice of entry mode. Journal of International Business Studies
aliases: Culture distance; Home-host cultural distance

name: Geographic distance
definition: The physical distance between the locations of two actors, such as a firm and its partner, target or subsidiary.
sign_convention: higher values mean the two actors are farther apart
citations: Ghemawat, P. (2001). Distance still matters: The hard reality of global expansion. Harvard Business Review
aliases: Spatial distance; Physical distance; Acquirer-target geographic distance; Distance between acquirer and target; Geographic distance in acquisitions; Geographic proximity; Geographic distance (reverse); Co-location; Spatial proximity; Same region

name: Temporal distance
definition: The separation between two locations arising from time zone differences, reflected in the number of overlapping working hours available for synchronous communication.
sign_convention: higher values mean fewer overlapping working hours between the two locations
aliases: Time zone distance; Business hour overlap

name: Liability of foreignness
definition: The additional costs and disadvantages that a firm operating in a host country faces relative to local firms because of its unfamiliarity with, and lack of roots in, the foreign environment.
sign_convention: higher values mean larger disadvantages of foreign relative to local firms
citations: Zaheer, S. (1995). Overcoming the liability of foreignness. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: LOF; Foreignness disadvantage

name: International strategy
definition: The configuration of a multinational firm's activities across countries, including how far it integrates and standardizes operations globally, adapts to local markets, and links its dispersed units.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more pronounced expression of the named strategic dimension
aliases: MNC strategy; Global strategy; MNC international strategy

name: Global integration
definition: The extent to which a firm or business unit rationalizes its worldwide activities through standardization of products and processes and centralized coordination across countries.
sign_convention: higher values mean more globally integrated and standardized operations
citations: Kobrin, S.J. (1991). An empirical analysis of the determinants of global integration. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Global integration of business activities; Global integration strategy

name: Marketing standardization
definition: The degree to which the elements of a firm's marketing program (product, price, distribution and promotion) are kept uniform across foreign markets rather than adapted locally.
sign_convention: higher values mean more standardized international marketing
citations: Jain, S.C. (1989). Standardization of international marketing strategy: Some research hypotheses. Journal of Marketing
aliases: International marketing strategy standardization

name: Local isomorphism
definition: The extent to which a foreign subsidiary adopts the practices and strategies of local domestic firms in the host country, as a way of gaining legitimacy and reducing the liability of foreignness.
sign_convention: higher values mean closer conformity to local firms' practices
citations: Salomon, R.; Wu, Z. (2012). Institutional distance and local isomorphism strategy. Journal of International Business Studies
aliases: Local isomorphism strategy

name: International interdependence
definition: The extent to which a multinational firm's units dispersed across countries are linked through flows of knowledge, products and resources.
sign_convention: higher values mean stronger cross-national linkages among the firm's units
citations: Ghoshal, S.; Bartlett, C.A. (1990). The multinational corporation as an interorganizational network. Academy of Management Review
aliases: Cross-national interdependence; Inter-subsidiary interdependence

name: Headquarters-subsidiary relationship
definition: The set of structural and relational arrangements between a multinational's headquarters and its foreign subsidiaries, including the mandate assigned to a subsidiary and the attention and control headquarters devotes to it.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more pronounced expression of the named relational dimension
citations: Birkinshaw, J.; Hood, N. (1998). Multinational subsidiary evolution: Capability and charter change in foreign-owned subsidiary companies. Academy of Management Review
aliases: HQ-subsidiary relations; Parent-subsidiary relationship

name: Headquarters attention
definition: The extent to which a multinational's headquarters recognizes, and gives credit to, a subsidiary for its contribution to the firm as a whole.
sign_convention: higher values mean more positive headquarters attention to the subsidiary
citations: Bouquet, C.; Birkinshaw, J. (2008). Weight versus voice: How foreign subsidiaries gain attention from corporate headquarters. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Positive headquarters attention; Relative attention

name: Subsidiary role
definition: The strategic mandate of a foreign subsidiary or unit within the multinational, in terms of the scope and nature of its responsibilities, from local adaptation to worldwide mandates.
sign_convention: higher values mean a broader, more global mandate for the unit
citations: Birkinshaw, J.; Hood, N. (1998). Multinational subsidiary evolution: Capability and charter change in foreign-owned subsidiary companies. Academy of Management Review
aliases: Subsidiary mandate; R&D unit role; R&D unit strategic mandate

name: Foreign subsidiary survival
definition: The continued operation of a foreign subsidiary in its host country over time, with exit by closure, liquidation or sale as the failure event. A parent's sale or spin-off of units analyzed as a corporate restructuring action is Divestiture.
sign_convention: higher values mean the subsidiary is more likely to survive (lower exit hazard)
citations: Delios, A.; Beamish, P.W. (2001). Survival and profitability: The roles of experience and intangible assets in foreign subsidiary performance. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Subsidiary survival

name: Cross-cultural adjustment
definition: The degree of psychological comfort an individual on an international assignment feels with the host environment, spanning general living conditions, interaction with host nationals and work.
sign_convention: higher values mean better adjustment to the host environment
citations: Black, J.S.; Mendenhall, M.; Oddou, G. (1991). Toward a comprehensive model of international adjustment: An integration of multiple theoretical perspectives. Academy of Management Review
aliases: Expatriate adjustment; International adjustment

name: Country of origin
definition: The home country or region in which a firm originates or is headquartered, used as a categorical marker of the national institutional and cultural context that shapes its behavior.
sign_convention: categorical; higher values mean membership in the focal home country or region
aliases: Firm nationality; Home country

name: Interorganizational relationship
definition: A voluntary, relatively enduring exchange or cooperative relationship between two or more organizations, such as a buyer-supplier relationship, an alliance, a joint venture or a client engagement. Umbrella for the existence and general attributes of such relationships.
sign_convention: higher values mean more or stronger interorganizational relationships
citations: Gulati, R. (1998). Alliances and networks. Strategic Management Journal; Uzzi, B. (1997). Social structure and competition in interfirm networks: The paradox of embeddedness. Administrative Science Quarterly
aliases: Interfirm relationship; Interorganizational relationships; Exchange relationship; Buyer-supplier relationship; Vertical relationship

name: Strategic alliance
definition: A voluntary cooperative agreement between independent firms involving the exchange, sharing or co-development of products, technologies or services, ranging from contractual agreements to equity joint ventures.
sign_convention: higher values mean more alliance involvement (presence or number of alliances)
citations: Gulati, R. (1998). Alliances and networks. Strategic Management Journal; Koza, M. P.; Lewin, A. Y. (1998). The co-evolution of strategic alliances. Organization Science
aliases: Alliance; Alliances; Strategic alliances; Interfirm alliance; Interfirm cooperative agreement; Joint venture; Partnership; Cooperative agreement

name: Alliance type
definition: The functional or strategic category of an alliance, such as scale versus link, marketing versus technology, or horizontal versus vertical, that characterizes the activities the partners pool.
sign_convention: higher values mean the alliance belongs to the reference category named by the study
citations: Koza, M. P.; Lewin, A. Y. (1998). The co-evolution of strategic alliances. Organization Science
aliases: Alliance category; Scale versus link alliance; Marketing versus technology alliance

name: Exploration alliance
definition: An alliance formed to discover new opportunities, technologies or competencies, typically upstream in research and development, as opposed to commercializing existing ones.
sign_convention: higher values mean more exploration alliances
citations: Koza, M. P.; Lewin, A. Y. (1998). The co-evolution of strategic alliances. Organization Science; Rothaermel, F. T.; Deeds, D. L. (2004). Exploration and exploitation alliances in biotechnology: A system of new product development. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Exploration alliances; Upstream alliances; R&D-stage alliances

name: Exploitation alliance
definition: An alliance formed to leverage and commercialize existing capabilities, typically downstream in development, manufacturing or marketing.
sign_convention: higher values mean more exploitation alliances
citations: Koza, M. P.; Lewin, A. Y. (1998). The co-evolution of strategic alliances. Organization Science; Rothaermel, F. T.; Deeds, D. L. (2004). Exploration and exploitation alliances in biotechnology: A system of new product development. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Exploitation alliances; Downstream alliances; Commercialization alliances

name: Alliance scope
definition: The breadth of functional activities, such as R&D, manufacturing and marketing, that partners agree to undertake together within an alliance.
sign_convention: higher values mean a broader alliance scope
citations: Reuer, J. J.; Arino, A. (2007). Strategic alliance contracts: Dimensions and determinants of contractual complexity. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Scope of the alliance; Breadth of alliance activities

name: Alliance size
definition: The number of partners participating in an alliance, syndicate or consortium, distinguishing bilateral from multilateral arrangements.
sign_convention: higher values mean more partners in the alliance
aliases: Number of partners; Multilateral alliance; Syndicate size; Multipartner alliance

name: Alliance governance structure
definition: The formal organizational arrangement chosen to organize an alliance, including the choice between equity and non-equity forms and the administrative devices that formalize joint control.
sign_convention: higher values mean more hierarchical (more formalized) alliance governance
citations: Gulati, R. (1995). Does familiarity breed trust? The implications of repeated ties for contractual choice in alliances. Academy of Management Journal; Williamson, O. E. (1991). Comparative economic organization: The analysis of discrete structural alternatives. Administrative Science Quarterly
aliases: Alliance governance; Alliance organizational form; Alliance governance form; Alliance design

name: Equity-based alliance governance
definition: Whether an alliance is governed through shared equity ownership (joint venture or minority equity stake) rather than through a purely contractual, non-equity agreement.
sign_convention: higher values mean equity-based governance rather than a non-equity contractual alliance
citations: Gulati, R. (1995). Does familiarity breed trust? The implications of repeated ties for contractual choice in alliances. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Equity use; Equity governance; Equity alliance; Joint venture versus contract; Equity joint venture; Nonequity alliance (reverse); Contractual alliance (reverse)

name: Alliance experience
definition: The accumulated experience a firm has gained from prior alliances, in general or with particular partners, that supports alliance management skill.
sign_convention: higher values mean more alliance experience
citations: Kale, P.; Dyer, J. H.; Singh, H. (2002). Alliance capability, stock market response, and long-term alliance success: The role of the alliance function. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Partnering experience; Collaborative experience

name: General alliance experience

name: Perceived founder ability
definition: An evaluator's assessment of a founder's capability to deliver on the venture's promises.
sign_convention: higher values mean the founder is perceived as more able
aliases: Perceived founder quality; Perceived founder skill; Perceived founder competence

name: Perceived preparedness
definition: An audience's perception that an entrepreneur has thoroughly prepared and understands the business idea, shown by the substance of the pitch and responses to questions; the cognitive component of perceived passion.
sign_convention: higher values mean the entrepreneur is perceived as better prepared
citations: Chen, X.-P.; Yao, X.; Kotha, S. (2009). Entrepreneur passion and preparedness in business plan presentations: A persuasion analysis of venture capitalists' funding decisions. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Preparedness of the presenter; Cognitive passion; Entrepreneur preparedness

name: Venture quality
definition: The overall quality of a new venture, summarizing the factors, including the idea, the team and the business plan, that drive its probability of success.
sign_convention: higher values mean a higher quality venture
citations: Arora, A.; Nandkumar, A. (2011). Cash-out or flameout! Opportunity cost and entrepreneurial strategy: Theory, and evidence from the information security industry. Management Science
aliases: Start-up quality; Quality of the venture; Venture potential

name: Business plan quality
definition: The thoroughness and persuasiveness with which a venture's business plan covers the opportunity, market, product, competition and financial prospects.
sign_convention: higher values mean a higher quality business plan
aliases: Quality of the business plan; Plan quality

name: Venture performance
definition: The performance of a new or entrepreneurial venture, assessed through its survival, growth, financial results and the achievement of milestones such as external financing and successful exit.
sign_convention: higher values mean better new venture performance
citations: Murphy, G. B.; Trailer, J. W.; Hill, R. C. (1996). Measuring performance in entrepreneurship research. Journal of Business Research
aliases: New venture performance; New firm performance; Start-up performance; Entrepreneurial performance; Venture success; Early-stage performance milestones

name: New venture survival
definition: Whether, or for how long, a new venture continues to operate rather than being dissolved, disbanded or failing.
sign_convention: higher values mean the venture survives or survives longer
citations: Delmar, F.; Shane, S. (2004). Legitimating first: Organizing activities and the survival of new ventures. Journal of Business Venturing
aliases: Venture survival; Startup survival; New firm survival; Probability of survival; Venture failure (reverse); Start-up failure (reverse); New venture failure (reverse); Venture disbanding (reverse); Dissolution (reverse); Liquidation (reverse)

name: New venture growth
definition: The rate at which a new venture expands its sales, employment or assets after founding.
sign_convention: higher values mean faster venture growth
citations: Delmar, F.; Davidsson, P.; Gartner, W. B. (2003). Arriving at the high-growth firm. Journal of Business Venturing
aliases: Venture growth; New firm growth; Venture growth performance; Start-up growth; Scaling

name: Successful venture exit
definition: A venture's transition to a liquidity event, an initial public offering or an acquisition, that returns capital to founders and investors and marks a performance milestone.
sign_convention: higher values mean the venture achieves a successful exit
citations: Shane, S.; Stuart, T. (2002). Organizational endowments and the performance of university start-ups. Management Science
aliases: Liquidity event; Venture exit; Cash-out; IPO or acquisition; Exit via IPO or acquisition

name: Initial public offering
definition: The event of a private firm first selling its shares to the public, which raises capital, provides liquidity to owners and marks a milestone of venture success.
sign_convention: higher values mean the firm completes an initial public offering
aliases: IPO; Going public; Initial public offerings; IPO completion

name: IPO underpricing
definition: The extent to which shares are sold in an initial public offering below the value the market assigns them, seen in the first-day price rise over the offer price.
sign_convention: higher values mean greater underpricing (larger first-day return)
citations: Ritter, J. R.; Welch, I. (2002). A review of IPO activity, pricing, and allocations. Journal of Finance
aliases: Underpricing; First-day return; Money left on the table; IPO discount
