name: Founding team size
definition: The number of individuals who together found a new venture and make up its initial founding team.
sign_convention: higher values mean more founders on the founding team
aliases: Number of founders; Number of cofounders; Size of the founding team; Founder team size; Founding team members

name: Public sector employment
definition: Whether an individual is employed in a government-owned or government-funded organization rather than in the private sector, treated as a feature of the person's employment context that shapes subsequent career moves such as entry into entrepreneurship.
sign_convention: higher values mean the individual is employed in the public sector
aliases: Public versus private sector employment; Government employment; Public sector employee; Prior public sector employment; Employment sector

name: Organizational environment
definition: The set of external conditions, actors and forces outside an organization's boundaries that affect its functioning, including the task environment (customers, competitors, suppliers, technology) and the general environment (economy, society). Umbrella entry that organizes the environmental dimensions and industry characteristics studied in the field.
sign_convention: umbrella entry; no single direction
citations: Dess, G. G.; Beard, D. W. (1984). Dimensions of organizational task environments. Administrative Science Quarterly
aliases: Environment; External environment; Task environment; Organizational task environment; Environmental characteristics; Environmental dimensions; General environment

name: Environmental dynamism
definition: The rate and unpredictability of change in an organization's external environment, including changes in customers, competitors and technology. Higher dynamism means faster and less predictable change, often labeled turbulence, volatility or instability.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more dynamic, turbulent or unstable environment
citations: Dess, G. G.; Beard, D. W. (1984). Dimensions of organizational task environments. Administrative Science Quarterly; Keats, B. W.; Hitt, M. A. (1988). A causal model of linkages among environmental dimensions, macro organizational characteristics, and performance. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Industry dynamism; Environmental turbulence; Environmental volatility; Environmental instability; Industry turbulence; Market turbulence; Sector dynamism; Perceived environmental dynamism

name: Industry velocity
definition: The pace or clockspeed at which an industry's conditions change, capturing how frequently its growth path and competitive parameters are altered. It is the rate component of environmental dynamism, distinguished from the magnitude of change.
sign_convention: higher values mean faster change in the industry
citations: Nadkarni, S.; Barr, P. S. (2008). Environmental context, managerial cognition, and strategic action: An integrated view. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Industry clockspeed; Environmental clockspeed; Rate of change; Environmental velocity

name: Technological dynamism
definition: The rate of change and unpredictability of the technologies relevant to a firm's industry. It is the technological component of environmental dynamism, often called technological turbulence.
sign_convention: higher values mean faster and less predictable technological change
citations: Jaworski, B. J.; Kohli, A. K. (1993). Market orientation: Antecedents and consequences. Journal of Marketing
aliases: Technological turbulence; Technological instability

name: Environmental munificence
definition: The extent to which an environment can support sustained growth and provides abundant resources and opportunities to the organizations within it. Scarce or resource-poor environments are the low pole.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more munificent, resource-rich environment
citations: Dess, G. G.; Beard, D. W. (1984). Dimensions of organizational task environments. Administrative Science Quarterly
aliases: Industry munificence; Market munificence; Environmental growth; Resource abundance; Environmental capacity

name: Environmental complexity
definition: The heterogeneity and range of elements in an organization's environment, such as the number and diversity of customers, competitors, markets and technologies it must attend to. Homogeneous, simple environments are the low pole.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more complex or heterogeneous environment
citations: Dess, G. G.; Beard, D. W. (1984). Dimensions of organizational task environments. Administrative Science Quarterly
aliases: Environmental heterogeneity; Industry complexity; Market complexity; Market heterogeneity; Perceived environmental complexity

name: Environmental hostility
definition: The degree to which an organization's environment is threatening, characterized by intense competition, scarce resources and unfavorable conditions that endanger the firm. Benign environments are the low pole. Decision makers' categorization of a specific strategic issue as a threat rather than an opportunity is Opportunity versus threat interpretation.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more hostile environment
citations: Miller, D.; Friesen, P. H. (1983). Strategy-making and environment: The third link. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Perceived environmental hostility; Environmental threat; Environmental adversity

name: Environmental change
definition: A discrete or cumulative shift in the conditions of an organization's environment, including jolts and discontinuities that alter competitive and operating conditions. It concerns the occurrence and nature of change rather than the ongoing rate of change captured by dynamism.
sign_convention: higher values mean more or larger environmental change has occurred
citations: Meyer, A. D. (1982). Adapting to environmental jolts. Administrative Science Quarterly
aliases: Environmental discontinuity; External context events; Environmental shift

name: Environmental shock
definition: A sudden, unanticipated and substantial change in an organization's environment, such as a regulatory, technological or economic discontinuity, that disrupts existing conditions. Typically coded as the presence of a shock period or event.
sign_convention: higher values mean a shock has occurred or is more severe
citations: Meyer, A. D. (1982). Adapting to environmental jolts. Administrative Science Quarterly
aliases: Exogenous shock; Environmental jolt; Crisis

name: Economic shock
definition: A severe, economy-wide environmental shock, such as a financial crisis or macroeconomic collapse, that raises the risk of failure across industries. A type of environmental shock originating in the macroeconomy.
sign_convention: higher values mean an economic shock is present
aliases: Macroeconomic shock; Financial crisis

name: Technological change
definition: Change in the technologies underlying an industry's products or processes, including technological shifts and discontinuities that redefine competition. A type of environmental change located in the technological environment.
sign_convention: higher values mean more technological change
aliases: Technological shift; Technological discontinuity

name: Magnitude of environmental change
definition: The size or severity of an environmental change, ranging from incremental variation to radical, second-order discontinuity. A dimension of environmental change distinct from its occurrence or frequency.
sign_convention: higher values mean larger or more severe change
aliases: Crisis severity; Severity of environmental change; Radicalness of environmental change

name: Technological environment
definition: The technological conditions surrounding an industry, including the opportunities for innovation and the intensity of technological activity in the sector. Umbrella for technology-related characteristics of the industry environment.
sign_convention: umbrella entry; no single direction
aliases: Industry technological environment

name: Technological opportunity
definition: The exogenous richness of an industry's or technical field's opportunities for innovation, reflecting differences across fields in the cost and ease of advancing technology. Higher technological opportunity means innovation is more productive.
sign_convention: higher values mean richer opportunities for technological advance
citations: Klevorick, A. K.; Levin, R. C.; Nelson, R. R.; Winter, S. G. (1995). On the sources and significance of interindustry differences in technological opportunities. Research Policy

name: Industry technology intensity
definition: The extent to which technological development and knowledge creation play a central role in an industry, as in high-technology or knowledge-intensive sectors. Usually indexed by the industry's R&D spending relative to sales.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more technology- or knowledge-intensive industry
aliases: Sector technology intensity; Industry knowledge intensity; Knowledge intensity; High-technology industry; Technological intensiveness

name: Industry R&D intensity
definition: The average ratio of research and development expenditure to sales across firms in an industry. A measure-named construct used as an indicator of industry technology intensity, differentiation and appropriability conditions.
sign_convention: higher values mean higher industry R&D spending relative to sales
aliases: Industry research intensity

name: Macroeconomic environment
definition: The economy-wide conditions that affect all organizations in a country, such as the business cycle, interest rates and labor market conditions. Umbrella for general-environment economic constructs.
sign_convention: umbrella entry; no single direction
aliases: Macroenvironmental factors; Macroeconomic activity

name: Macroeconomic conditions
definition: The overall state of the economy in which a firm operates, reflecting the phase of the business cycle and the level of economic activity and growth. Downturns and recessions are the low pole.
sign_convention: higher values mean more favorable economic conditions
aliases: State of the economy; Economic conditions; Business cycle; Economic growth; Stock market cycle

name: Interest rate
definition: The prevailing cost of capital in an economy, typically the prime or benchmark lending rate. A macroeconomic condition affecting investment and strategic change.
sign_convention: higher values mean a higher cost of capital
aliases: Interest rates; Cost of capital (macro)

name: Unemployment rate
definition: The share of the labor force that is unemployed in a region or country, indicating labor market slack. A macroeconomic labor market condition.
sign_convention: higher values mean more unemployment
aliases: Local unemployment

name: Demand conditions
definition: The characteristics of demand for an industry's or firm's products, including the size of the market and the level of demand. Umbrella for demand-side environment constructs other than demand uncertainty.
sign_convention: umbrella entry; no single direction
aliases: Demand environment; Market demand conditions

name: Market size
definition: The size of the market a firm or industry serves, in terms of the number of potential buyers, population or total sales volume. Larger markets offer greater potential returns to entry and innovation.
sign_convention: higher values mean a larger market
aliases: Extent of the market; Market potential; Market capacity

name: Demand level
definition: The level of realized or expected demand for a product, industry or location, reflected in sales, usage, adoption or popularity. Distinct from market size, which concerns potential buyers.
sign_convention: higher values mean more demand
aliases: Product demand; Industry demand; Local demand; Consumer demand; Market adoption; Product popularity

name: Agglomeration
definition: The geographic concentration of economic activity in an industry or technical field, such as clusters of firms or inventors in a location. Captures the collocation of related activity and the externalities it generates.
sign_convention: higher values mean more geographic concentration of activity
citations: Ellison, G.; Glaeser, E. L. (1997). Geographic concentration in U.S. manufacturing industries: A dartboard approach. Journal of Political Economy
aliases: Geographic clustering; Industrial cluster; Innovation hub; Location in a cluster

name: Internal agglomeration
definition: The geographic clustering of establishments owned by the same parent firm, generating intrafirm proximity benefits. A form of agglomeration that occurs within rather than between firms.
sign_convention: higher values mean more collocation of the firm's own establishments
aliases: Internal agglomerations; Intrafirm collocation

name: Resource dependence
definition: The extent to which an organization depends on external actors, markets or resource pools for critical inputs, which constrains its autonomy and shapes its strategies. Includes dependence on a particular market for revenue.
sign_convention: higher values mean greater dependence on external parties or markets
citations: Pfeffer, J.; Salancik, G. R. (1978). The External Control of Organizations: A Resource Dependence Perspective. Harper & Row (book)
aliases: Market dependence; External dependence

name: Environmental sector
definition: The distinct sectors of an organization's task and general environment, such as customers, competitors, suppliers, technology, regulators and the economy, that managers monitor and respond to. A categorical construct identifying which sector is at issue.
sign_convention: categorical; no directional convention
citations: Daft, R. L.; Sormunen, J.; Parks, D. (1988). Chief executive scanning, environmental characteristics, and company performance: An empirical study. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Task environment sector; Environment sector; Organizational task environment sector

name: Industry structure
definition: The structural characteristics of an industry that shape the nature and intensity of competition and the profit potential of its members, including concentration, entry barriers, growth, profitability, differentiation and cost structure. Umbrella from the industrial organization tradition.
sign_convention: umbrella entry; no single direction
citations: Porter, M. E. (1980). Competitive Strategy: Techniques for Analyzing Industries and Competitors. Free Press (book); Bain, J. S. (1956). Barriers to New Competition. Harvard University Press (book)
aliases: Industry characteristics; Industry conditions; Industry context; Market structure; Product market conditions; Product market characteristics; Competitive environment

name: Industry concentration
definition: The degree to which an industry's or market's output is accounted for by a small number of firms. Fragmented markets with many small sellers are the low pole.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more concentrated market
citations: Bain, J. S. (1956). Barriers to New Competition. Harvard University Press (book)
aliases: Market concentration; Seller concentration; Degree of concentration; Market dominance; Herfindahl index; Four-firm concentration ratio

name: Competitive forces
definition: The set of forces that jointly determine the intensity of competition and profitability in an industry: rivalry among existing firms, threat of new entrants, bargaining power of buyers, bargaining power of suppliers and threat of substitutes. Umbrella following Porter's framework.
sign_convention: umbrella entry; no single direction
citations: Porter, M. E. (1980). Competitive Strategy: Techniques for Analyzing Industries and Competitors. Free Press (book)
aliases: Porter's five competitive forces; Five forces

name: Product market competition
definition: The intensity of competition among firms in a product market, reflecting how strongly rivals contest customers and profits through price, quality and other competitive moves. Monopoly or weak rivalry is the low pole.
sign_convention: higher values mean more intense competition
citations: Porter, M. E. (1980). Competitive Strategy: Techniques for Analyzing Industries and Competitors. Free Press (book)
aliases: Competitive intensity; Industry competition; Market competition; Degree of competition; Intensity of competition; Industry rivalry; Industry competitiveness; Competitive pressure

name: Hypercompetition
definition: An environment characterized by intense and rapid competitive moves in which advantages are quickly eroded, so that firms must continually build new advantages. A type of especially intense and dynamic product market competition.
sign_convention: higher values mean more hypercompetitive conditions
citations: D'Aveni, R. A. (1994). Hypercompetition: Managing the Dynamics of Strategic Maneuvering. Free Press (book)

name: Import competition
definition: The intensity of competition that domestic firms face from foreign producers, typically indexed by import penetration of the industry. A type of product market competition originating abroad.
sign_convention: higher values mean more competition from imports
aliases: Foreign competition; Import penetration; Foreign import intensity; Foreign-based competition

name: Informal competition
definition: Competitive pressure from unregistered, informal-sector firms that sell legal goods while avoiding regulation and taxes. A type of product market competition characteristic of emerging economies.
sign_convention: higher values mean more competition from informal firms
aliases: Threat from informal sector firms; Informal sector competition

name: Buyer power
definition: The bargaining power of a firm's customers relative to the firm, arising from customer concentration, dependence on major customers and buyers' ability to switch. One of the competitive forces.
sign_convention: higher values mean more powerful buyers
citations: Porter, M. E. (1980). Competitive Strategy: Techniques for Analyzing Industries and Competitors. Free Press (book)
aliases: Customer power; Customer concentration; Bargaining power of buyers

name: Supplier power
definition: The bargaining power of suppliers relative to the buying firm, which is high when few alternative suppliers or products are available. One of the competitive forces; competition among suppliers is its inverse.
sign_convention: higher values mean more powerful suppliers
citations: Porter, M. E. (1980). Competitive Strategy: Techniques for Analyzing Industries and Competitors. Free Press (book)
aliases: Bargaining power of suppliers

name: Threat of new entry
definition: The likelihood that new competitors will enter a market and erode incumbents' positions. One of the competitive forces; it is lower when entry barriers are high.
sign_convention: higher values mean a greater threat of entry
citations: Porter, M. E. (1980). Competitive Strategy: Techniques for Analyzing Industries and Competitors. Free Press (book)
aliases: Threat of potential entry; Potential rivalry; Entry threat; Threat of entry; Potential competition; Potential entry

name: Barriers to entry
definition: Structural conditions such as scale economies, capital requirements, product differentiation and brand loyalty that make entry into an industry costly or difficult for new firms.
sign_convention: higher values mean higher barriers to entry
citations: Bain, J. S. (1956). Barriers to New Competition. Harvard University Press (book)
aliases: Industry entry barriers; Entry barriers

name: Minimum efficient scale
definition: The smallest scale of production at which unit costs reach their minimum, indicating the importance of scale economies in an industry. A structural source of entry barriers and of production concentration.
sign_convention: higher values mean larger minimum efficient scale
citations: Bain, J. S. (1956). Barriers to New Competition. Harvard University Press (book)
aliases: Plant minimum efficient scale; Minimum efficient scale of production

name: Organizational density
definition: The number of organizations in a population, market or niche, as theorized in organizational ecology to capture legitimation and competition processes. Counts of rivals used as proxies for the intensity of rivalry in a product market measure Product market competition instead.
sign_convention: higher values mean more organizations in the population or market
citations: Carroll, G. R.; Hannan, M. T. (1989). Density dependence in the evolution of populations of newspaper organizations. American Sociological Review
aliases: Population density (ecology); Market density; Local density; Category crowdedness; Density; Founding density

name: Niche-overlap density
definition: Population density weighted by the degree to which other organizations' resource niches overlap with the focal organization's niche, capturing localized competition. A refinement of organizational density.
sign_convention: higher values mean more overlapping competitors
citations: Baum, J. A. C.; Singh, J. V. (1994). Organizational niches and the dynamics of organizational mortality. American Journal of Sociology
aliases: Overlap density; Organizational niche overlap density; Platform overlap density

name: Industry growth
definition: The rate of growth in the sales, output or demand of an industry or market over time. A structural industry characteristic and the standard indicator of environmental munificence.
sign_convention: higher values mean faster industry or market growth
aliases: Industry growth rate; Market growth; Market growth rate; Demand growth; Industry demand growth; Perceived industry growth

name: Industry life cycle stage
definition: The stage of an industry or product market in its life cycle, from emergence and growth through maturity to decline, which structures demand growth, competition and innovation. Industry age is a common proxy.
sign_convention: higher values mean a later, more mature stage
citations: Klepper, S. (1996). Entry, exit, growth, and innovation over the product life cycle. American Economic Review
aliases: Industry life cycle phase; Product life cycle stage; Industry maturity; Industry age; Technology maturity

name: Industry profitability
definition: The average profitability of the firms in an industry or market, indicating the industry's economic returns and attractiveness to entrants.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more profitable industry
aliases: Industry performance; Market profitability; Industry return on assets

name: Industry attractiveness
definition: The overall economic attractiveness of an industry or market as a place to compete or invest, combining its profit potential, growth and favorable conditions. A summary evaluation of industry structure.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more attractive industry or market
citations: Porter, M. E. (1980). Competitive Strategy: Techniques for Analyzing Industries and Competitors. Free Press (book)
aliases: Core industry attractiveness; Industry financial attractiveness; Market attractiveness

name: Industry differentiation
definition: The extent to which products in an industry are differentiated among competitors, so that competition is based on distinct product attributes rather than price alone. Typically indexed by industry advertising or R&D intensity.
sign_convention: higher values mean more product differentiation in the industry
aliases: Industry product differentiation; Product differentiation (industry)

name: Industry advertising intensity
definition: The average ratio of advertising expenditure to sales across firms in an industry. A measure-named construct used as an indicator of industry product differentiation and entry barriers.
sign_convention: higher values mean higher industry advertising relative to sales
citations: Comanor, W. S.; Wilson, T. A. (1967). Advertising, market structure and performance. Review of Economics and Statistics

name: Industry capital intensity
definition: The relative investment in fixed assets required to operate in an industry, typically the ratio of fixed assets or investment to sales. Indicates scale barriers and the capital commitment needed for entry.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more capital-intensive industry
aliases: Investment intensity; Capital intensity (industry)

name: Industry labor intensity
definition: The amount of labor used relative to output or sales in an industry, indicating how central labor is to the industry's production.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more labor-intensive industry
aliases: Labor intensity

name: Industry unionization
definition: The rate of union membership among workers in an industry, indicating collective worker power in the industry's labor market.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more unionized industry
aliases: Unionization rate; Union density

name: Industry learning intensity
definition: The importance of learning by doing in an industry, reflected in how strongly cumulative production experience lowers costs or raises productivity. A production-technology characteristic of the industry environment.
sign_convention: higher values mean stronger learning-by-doing effects in the industry
citations: Balasubramanian, N.; Lieberman, M. B. (2010). Industry learning environments and the heterogeneity of firm performance. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Industry learning-by-doing rate; Industry learning environment

name: Industry globalization
definition: The extent of linkages among national markets in an industry, in terms of international trade, cross-border production and the geographic scope of the relevant market.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more globalized industry
citations: Wiersema, M. F.; Bowen, H. P. (2008). Corporate diversification: The impact of foreign competition, industry globalization, and product diversification. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Globalization of markets and industries

name: Uncertainty
definition: The inability to predict future states or outcomes accurately because of incomplete information, whether the source is the external environment, the firm's own decisions or the transaction at hand. Umbrella for uncertainty constructs.
sign_convention: higher values mean less ability to predict
citations: Milliken, F. J. (1987). Three types of uncertainty about the environment: State, effect, and response uncertainty. Academy of Management Review
aliases: Uncertainty (general); Outcome uncertainty; Transaction uncertainty; Uncertainty

name: Environmental uncertainty
definition: The inability of decision makers to predict the state of the external environment accurately, arising from its dynamism, complexity and volatility. Measured either as managers' perceptions or as objective variability in industry conditions.
sign_convention: higher values mean a less predictable environment
citations: Milliken, F. J. (1987). Three types of uncertainty about the environment: State, effect, and response uncertainty. Academy of Management Review; Duncan, R. B. (1972). Characteristics of organizational environments and perceived environmental uncertainty. Administrative Science Quarterly
aliases: External uncertainty; Industry uncertainty; Exogenous uncertainty; Strategic uncertainty; Industry-level uncertainty; Environmental unpredictability; Environmental predictability; Predictability of customer demands and competitor actions

name: Market uncertainty
definition: Uncertainty about demand and market conditions for a firm's products, driven by exogenous factors such as the economic cycle and shifting customer preferences. A type of environmental uncertainty located in the market sector.
sign_convention: higher values mean less predictable market conditions
citations: Beckman, C. M.; Haunschild, P. R.; Phillips, D. J. (2004). Friends or strangers? Firm-specific uncertainty, market uncertainty, and network partner selection. Organization Science
aliases: Exogenous market uncertainty; Commercial uncertainty

name: Demand uncertainty
definition: The unpredictability of the level of demand for an industry's or firm's products. A type of market uncertainty concerning quantity demanded.
sign_convention: higher values mean less predictable demand
aliases: Industry demand uncertainty; Demand unpredictability; Volume uncertainty

name: Demand variability
definition: The magnitude of fluctuation in demand over time, distinguished from its predictability. A component of demand uncertainty that is often used as its measure.
sign_convention: higher values mean larger fluctuations in demand
aliases: Demand variation; Demand volatility; Industry demand volatility

name: Technological uncertainty
definition: Limited knowledge about the future development, performance and payoffs of technologies relevant to a firm. A type of environmental uncertainty located in the technological sector.
sign_convention: higher values mean less predictable technology outcomes
aliases: Technical uncertainty; Development uncertainty; Technological uncertainty

name: Competitive uncertainty
definition: Uncertainty arising from the actions of actual or potential competitors, including entry, innovation and strategic moves. A type of environmental uncertainty located in the competitor sector.
sign_convention: higher values mean less predictable competitor actions
citations: Sutcliffe, K. M.; Zaheer, A. (1998). Uncertainty in the transaction environment: An empirical test. Strategic Management Journal

name: Macroeconomic uncertainty
definition: Uncertainty about aggregate economic prospects, reflected in the volatility of economy-wide shocks, GDP growth or aggregate market returns. A type of environmental uncertainty located in the general economy.
sign_convention: higher values mean more uncertain macroeconomic conditions
aliases: Aggregate volatility; Aggregate uncertainty

name: Firm-specific uncertainty
definition: Lack of assurance about the probability and outcomes of a firm's own decisions, stemming from idiosyncratic sources rather than the shared environment. Distinct from market uncertainty; often indexed by firm stock volatility or analyst forecast dispersion.
sign_convention: higher values mean more idiosyncratic uncertainty about the firm
citations: Beckman, C. M.; Haunschild, P. R.; Phillips, D. J. (2004). Friends or strangers? Firm-specific uncertainty, market uncertainty, and network partner selection. Organization Science
aliases: Idiosyncratic uncertainty; Information uncertainty; Analyst forecast dispersion

name: Time trend
definition: The passage of calendar time or the position of an observation in a sequence of periods, used to capture secular trends or period effects that are not attributed to a specific environmental construct.
sign_convention: higher values mean a later time or period
aliases: Time; Time period; Calendar time; Year; Period effect

name: Industry membership
definition: The industry or sector to which a firm belongs, as a categorical classification (for example SIC or NAICS groups). Captures industry fixed effects and industry-based contingencies without specifying a particular industry attribute.
sign_convention: categorical; no directional convention
aliases: Industry; Industry type; Industry dummies; Industry category; Industry sector

name: Manufacturing versus service sector
definition: Whether a firm or organization operates in the service sector rather than in manufacturing or goods production. A binary industry classification.
sign_convention: higher values mean the service sector rather than manufacturing
aliases: Industrial sector; Service versus manufacturing; Percentage of units in manufacturing

name: Consumer-facing industry
definition: Whether a firm operates in an industry that sells goods or services directly to individual consumers rather than to businesses. A binary industry classification.
sign_convention: higher values mean a business-to-consumer industry
aliases: Consumer orientation; Business-to-consumer sector; Consumer-focused industry; B2C industry

name: Search versus experience goods
definition: The degree to which the quality of an industry's products or services can be evaluated by buyers before purchase (search qualities) rather than only after purchase or use (experience and credence qualities), which determines the information asymmetry between sellers and buyers.
sign_convention: higher values mean quality is harder to assess before purchase (experience or credence rather than search qualities)
citations: Nelson, P. (1970). Information and consumer behavior. Journal of Political Economy; Darby, M. R.; Karni, E. (1973). Free competition and the optimal amount of fraud. Journal of Law and Economics
aliases: Experience goods; Search goods; Service characteristics (search versus experience); Experience versus search services; Credence goods

name: Community ethnic diversity
definition: The heterogeneity of the racial or ethnic composition of the population in the local community or region in which an organization operates, treated as a feature of its social environment.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more ethnically heterogeneous local population
aliases: Community racial diversity; Local ethnic diversity; Ethnic diversity of the community; Community social diversity

name: External finance dependence
definition: The extent to which firms in an industry must rely on external funds rather than internally generated cash flow to finance their investment, a technological characteristic of the industry that determines its sensitivity to financial market conditions.
sign_convention: higher values mean the industry depends more on external finance
citations: Rajan, R. G.; Zingales, L. (1998). Financial dependence and growth. American Economic Review
aliases: External financial dependence; Dependence on external finance; External funds dependence; External equity dependence; Rajan-Zingales financial dependence

name: Institutional environment
definition: The set of formal rules (laws, regulations, political institutions) and informal norms that structure economic and organizational activity in a country or region. Umbrella for the regulative, normative and political features of the institutional context that firms face.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more developed, stable and market-supporting institutional environment
citations: North, D. C. (1990). Institutions, Institutional Change and Economic Performance. Cambridge University Press (book); Scott, W. R. (1995). Institutions and Organizations. Sage (book)
aliases: Institutional context; National institutional environment; Institutional profile; National context; Institutional infrastructure

name: Institutional development
definition: The degree to which formal market-supporting institutions such as property rights, contract enforcement, rule of law and functioning factor markets are present and effective in a country or region. Low values correspond to institutional voids.
sign_convention: higher values mean more developed and stronger market-supporting institutions (fewer institutional voids)
citations: Khanna, T.; Palepu, K. (1997). Why focused strategies may be right for emerging markets. Harvard Business Review
aliases: Level of institutional development; Institutional quality; Market-supporting institutions; Strength of market institutions; Institutional voids (reverse); Subnational institutional development; Marketization

name: Public governance quality
definition: The quality of a country's public governance, including rule of law, control of corruption, government effectiveness, regulatory quality and political stability, as captured by cross-national governance indicators.
sign_convention: higher values mean better public governance and stronger national institutions
citations: Kaufmann, D.; Kraay, A.; Mastruzzi, M. (2011). The Worldwide Governance Indicators: Methodology and analytical issues. Hague Journal on the Rule of Law
aliases: Quality of governance; Governance quality

name: Financial market development
definition: The depth, breadth and governance quality of a country's or region's capital and credit markets, which determine how easily firms can obtain external financing.
sign_convention: higher values mean more developed financial and capital markets and easier access to external finance
aliases: Capital market development; Regional financial development; Financial development

name: Corruption
definition: The extent to which public officials abuse public power for private gain and the likelihood that firms encounter demands for bribes or other corrupt transactions in their dealings with the state.
sign_convention: higher values mean more corruption
citations: Rodriguez, P.; Uhlenbruck, K.; Eden, L. (2005). Government corruption and the entry strategies of multinationals. Academy of Management Review
aliases: Perceived corruption; Host country corruption; Home country corruption; Pervasive corruption; Corruption pervasiveness

name: Legal environment
definition: The body of laws and legal enforcement institutions that define and protect the rights of economic actors in a jurisdiction, and the degree to which that legal system is developed and enforced.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more developed and better enforced legal system
citations: La Porta, R.; Lopez-de-Silanes, F.; Shleifer, A.; Vishny, R. W. (1998). Law and finance. Journal of Political Economy
aliases: Legal development; Law development; Legal institutions; Rule of law; Corporate legal environment

name: Intellectual property protection
definition: The strength of the legal regime that protects intellectual property, in particular the extent to which patents and related rights effectively prevent imitation and appropriation of a firm's knowledge.
sign_convention: higher values mean stronger intellectual property protection
citations: Levin, R. C.; Klevorick, A. K.; Nelson, R. R.; Winter, S. G. (1987). Appropriating the returns from industrial research and development. Brookings Papers on Economic Activity
aliases: Intellectual property rights protection; IP regime strength; Patent effectiveness; Strength of patent protection; Strength of knowledge protection; Appropriability regime (legal)

name: Creditor rights
definition: The extent to which a country's laws protect lenders, for example by giving secured creditors priority in liquidation and allowing them to enforce claims against defaulting debtors.
sign_convention: higher values mean stronger legal protection of creditors
citations: La Porta, R.; Lopez-de-Silanes, F.; Shleifer, A.; Vishny, R. W. (1998). Law and finance. Journal of Political Economy
aliases: Creditor rights protection; Creditor protection

name: Shareholder litigation risk
definition: The extent to which a firm's managers and directors are exposed to lawsuits by shareholders, as determined by the legal rules of the firm's jurisdiction that make derivative and securities suits easier or harder to bring.
sign_convention: higher values mean greater exposure of the firm to shareholder litigation
aliases: Litigation risk; Universal demand law (reverse); Derivative lawsuit exposure

name: Labor market institutions
definition: The laws, collective arrangements and social insurance provisions that govern the employment relationship in a jurisdiction, shaping the cost of hiring, dismissing and retaining workers and the bargaining power of employees.
sign_convention: higher values mean labor institutions that more strongly protect or empower workers relative to employers
citations: Botero, J. C.; Djankov, S.; La Porta, R.; Lopez-de-Silanes, F.; Shleifer, A. (2004). The regulation of labor. Quarterly Journal of Economics
aliases: Labor regulations; Strength of labor institutions; Labor market frictions; Institutional labor market frictions

name: Employment protection
definition: The strength of legal rules that protect employees from dismissal and exploitation, raising the cost to employers of terminating or deviating from the employment contract.
sign_convention: higher values mean stronger legal protection of employees
citations: Botero, J. C.; Djankov, S.; La Porta, R.; Lopez-de-Silanes, F.; Shleifer, A. (2004). The regulation of labor. Quarterly Journal of Economics
aliases: Employment protection laws; Employee rights; Worker rights protection; Labor protection laws; Wrongful discharge laws

name: Noncompete enforceability
definition: The degree to which a jurisdiction's law enforces post-employment covenants not to compete, restricting employees' ability to move to or found competing firms.
sign_convention: higher values mean stricter enforcement of noncompete agreements
citations: Marx, M.; Strumsky, D.; Fleming, L. (2009). Mobility, skills, and the Michigan non-compete experiment. Management Science
aliases: Non-compete enforceability; Non-compete covenant enforceability; Noncompete agreement enforceability; Non-compete enforcement; Covenants not to compete

name: Unionization
definition: The extent to which the labor force in a country or other jurisdiction is organized in trade unions. Union membership rates within an industry are Industry unionization.
sign_convention: higher values mean a larger share of workers enrolled in unions
aliases: Union density; Trade union membership

name: Unemployment insurance generosity
definition: The level of income support that the public unemployment insurance system provides to workers who lose their jobs, which lowers the private cost of job loss.
sign_convention: higher values mean more generous unemployment benefits
aliases: UI benefit generosity; Unemployment benefits

name: Wage bargaining centralization
definition: The degree to which wage setting is governed by centralized collective bargaining rather than by decentralized, flexible negotiation at the firm or individual level.
sign_convention: higher values mean more centralized collective wage bargaining
aliases: Centralization of wage bargaining; Decentralized wage bargaining (reverse)

name: Regulatory environment
definition: The rules, laws and regulatory agencies through which the state constrains and directs organizational activity, corresponding to the regulative pillar of the institutional environment.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more extensive and influential regulatory regime
citations: Kostova, T.; Roth, K. (2002). Adoption of an organizational practice by subsidiaries of multinational corporations: Institutional and relational effects. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Regulative institutional pillar; Regulatory institutional profile; Regulative institutional pressures; Regulatory institutions; Regulative elements

name: Industry regulation
definition: The extent to which an industry's activities, prices, entry or conduct are subject to government regulation, so that firms in it depend on government policy and regulatory approval.
sign_convention: higher values mean the industry is more heavily regulated
citations: Stigler, G. J. (1971). The theory of economic regulation. Bell Journal of Economics and Management Science
aliases: Government regulation; Industrial regulation; Regulated industry; Degree of regulation

name: Regulatory stringency
definition: The strictness and restrictiveness of the regulations that apply to an organization, that is, how much regulation limits permissible activities and how demanding compliance is.
sign_convention: higher values mean stricter, more restrictive regulation
aliases: Regulatory restrictiveness; Regulatory constraints; State environmental stringency; Stringency of regulation

name: Regulatory uncertainty
definition: The unpredictability of the regulatory environment facing decision makers, arising from new legislation and unforeseeable changes in existing regulations and their enforcement.
sign_convention: higher values mean greater uncertainty about future regulation
aliases: Regulatory risk; Economic policy uncertainty

name: Regulatory discretion
definition: The freedom of regulatory agencies to interpret and implement the policies written by elected officials, as determined by the institutional arrangements between politicians and regulators.
sign_convention: higher values mean regulators have more discretion in implementing policy
aliases: Agency discretion; Bureaucratic discretion

name: Regulatory pressure
definition: Formal, coercive pressure exerted on an organization by government, regulatory and legislative actors to conform to legal and policy standards, for example through regulatory scrutiny, inspection intensity and political demands. Sanctions for the firm's own violations, such as fines or enforcement actions for wrongdoing, indicate Corporate misconduct.
sign_convention: higher values mean stronger coercive pressure from regulatory and political actors
aliases: Regulatory pressures; Formal regulatory forces; Coercive pressure; Political stakeholder pressure

name: Regulatory approval
definition: A regulatory agency's favorable decision on an organization's petition, license or application, granting permission to undertake a regulated activity.
sign_convention: higher values mean the regulator approved the request (or approval is more likely or faster)
aliases: License approval; Petition approval; Regulatory agency decision

name: Political environment
definition: The political institutions and political conditions of a country or jurisdiction, including the constraints on policymakers, the competitiveness of politics, the degree of democracy and the state of public opinion.
sign_convention: no single direction: a heading for unlike political conditions; each finding keeps the direction of its own measure
aliases: Political institutions; Political character of the home country; Home country policy-making environment

name: Political risk
definition: The extent to which a host country's political conditions, including weak institutional constraints on policymakers, policy instability and political violence, threaten firms' operations and investment returns.
sign_convention: higher values mean greater political hazard and policy uncertainty
citations: Henisz, W. J. (2000). The institutional environment for economic growth. Economics and Politics; Henisz, W. J.; Delios, A. (2001). Uncertainty, imitation, and plant location: Japanese multinational corporations, 1990-1996. Administrative Science Quarterly
aliases: Political hazards; Policy uncertainty; Political uncertainty; Host country risk; Political instability; Policy stability (reverse); Political constraints (reverse)

name: Political competition
definition: The intensity of competition among political actors, parties or candidates for office and policy control, including partisan competition among veto players and closeness of elections.
sign_convention: higher values mean more intense competition among political actors
citations: Bonardi, J.-P.; Hillman, A. J.; Keim, G. D. (2005). The attractiveness of political markets: Implications for firm strategy. Academy of Management Review
aliases: Political competitiveness; Rivalry between elected politicians; Partisan competition; Electoral competition

name: Political democracy
definition: The extent to which a country's political system grants citizens civil liberties and political rights and limits the discretionary power of government over its citizenry.
sign_convention: higher values mean more democratic political institutions
aliases: Political freedom; Democracy; Regional political democracy

name: Public opinion
definition: The prevalent views and preferences of the general public toward an issue, policy or organization, which shape the political and social pressure organizations face.
sign_convention: higher values mean stronger public support for the focal issue, policy or organization
aliases: Public support; Public sentiment

name: Normative institutional environment
definition: The shared values, norms and beliefs in a society that define socially appropriate conduct, corresponding to the normative pillar of the institutional environment.
sign_convention: higher values mean stronger normative pressure toward the focal norm
citations: Kostova, T.; Roth, K. (2002). Adoption of an organizational practice by subsidiaries of multinational corporations: Institutional and relational effects. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Normative institutional profile; Normative institutional pressures; Informal institutions; Normative pillar

name: Norm enforcement
definition: The degree to which violations of social or business norms are sanctioned by third parties through informal punishments such as gossip, ostracism, economic penalties or other retaliation.
sign_convention: higher values mean norm violations are more reliably and severely punished
aliases: Norm enforcement in business communities; Confidence in enforcement of business norms; Informal sanctions; Third-party punishment

name: Institutional logics
definition: The socially constructed patterns of practices, assumptions, values and beliefs by which actors in a field organize activity and give meaning to it; a field may be governed by one dominant logic or by several competing logics.
sign_convention: higher values mean the focal logic is more dominant in the field
citations: Thornton, P. H.; Ocasio, W. (1999). Institutional logics and the historical contingency of power in organizations: Executive succession in the higher education publishing industry, 1958-1990. American Journal of Sociology
aliases: Field-level institutional logic; Institutional logic; Field-level logic; Dominant logic of the field

name: State logic
definition: The institutional logic that legitimates regulation of individual and organizational activity through state command-and-control, law and bureaucratic hierarchy; its prevalence reflects the role of the state relative to the market in an economy.
sign_convention: higher values mean a stronger state logic (greater state involvement relative to market logic)
aliases: State institutional logic; Government logic

name: Institutional complexity
definition: The condition in which an organization or field faces incompatible prescriptions from multiple institutional logics, so that realizing one logic's goals undermines another's.
sign_convention: higher values mean more conflicting institutional logics
citations: Greenwood, R.; Raynard, M.; Kodeih, F.; Micelotta, E. R.; Lounsbury, M. (2011). Institutional complexity and organizational responses. Academy of Management Annals
aliases: Institutional pluralism; Logic conflict

name: Institutional change
definition: A shift in the institutional arrangements of a field, industry or society, such as new laws, property rights, policy regimes or legitimate practices, that alters the rules of the game for organizations.
sign_convention: higher values mean the institutional change has occurred or is more extensive
citations: Greenwood, R.; Suddaby, R. (2006). Institutional entrepreneurship in mature fields: The Big Five accounting firms. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Institutional regime change; Institutional transition

name: Regulatory change
definition: A change in the laws, regulations or policies that govern an industry or activity, such as the introduction, tightening or revision of regulatory requirements or payment rules.
sign_convention: higher values mean the regulatory change has taken effect (or is larger)
aliases: Policy change; Legislative change; Regulatory tightening; Regulatory shock; Regulatory reform

name: Deregulation
definition: The removal or substantial reduction of government regulation of an industry, replacing administered control with competitive market principles.
sign_convention: higher values mean more deregulation (regulation removed or reduced)
aliases: Industry deregulation; Retail deregulation; Liberalization

name: Promarket reforms
definition: Policy reforms that reduce government intervention in the economy and strengthen market mechanisms, such as privatization, liberalization of trade and investment, and deregulation, typically in developing or transition economies.
sign_convention: higher values mean more extensive pro-market reform (a later stage of market transition)
citations: Cuervo-Cazurra, A.; Dau, L. A. (2009). Promarket reforms and firm profitability in developing countries. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Pro-market reforms; Economic reform; Market transition; Stage of reform; Economic liberalization

name: Institutional distance
definition: The difference between the institutional environments of two countries, typically the home and host country of a multinational firm, across regulative, normative and cognitive dimensions.
sign_convention: higher values mean larger institutional differences between the two countries
citations: Kostova, T.; Zaheer, S. (1999). Organizational legitimacy under conditions of complexity: The case of the multinational enterprise. Academy of Management Review
aliases: Regulatory distance; Institutional difference; Home-host institutional similarity (reverse)

name: Bilateral political relations
definition: The state of political relations between two countries, reflecting the alignment of their national interests and their history of cooperation or conflict.
sign_convention: higher values mean friendlier, more aligned political relations between the two countries
aliases: Interstate relations; Political relations between countries

name: Political affinity
definition: The similarity of two countries' national interests in global affairs, indicating how politically aligned their governments are.
sign_convention: higher values mean greater political alignment between the two countries
aliases: Level of political affinity; UN voting similarity; Political alignment

name: Historical interstate conflict
definition: The extent to which two countries have a history of wars, crises or other militarized conflict with each other.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more conflictual shared history between the two countries
aliases: Nation-dyadic historical conflict; Interstate conflict history

name: Corporate political activity
definition: Corporate attempts to shape government policy in ways favorable to the firm, through tactics such as lobbying, campaign contributions, testimony and participation in collective political action.
sign_convention: higher values mean more corporate political activity
citations: Hillman, A. J.; Hitt, M. A. (1999). Corporate political strategy formulation: A model of approach, participation, and strategy decisions. Academy of Management Review; Hillman, A. J.; Keim, G. D.; Schuler, D. (2004). Corporate political activity: A review and research agenda. Journal of Management
aliases: Corporate political strategy; Corporate political tactics; CPA; Nonmarket strategy (political)

name: Lobbying
definition: A firm's direct efforts to influence legislators and regulators by communicating information and arguments, usually captured by the resources it devotes to registered lobbying.
sign_convention: higher values mean more lobbying activity
citations: Hillman, A. J.; Hitt, M. A. (1999). Corporate political strategy formulation: A model of approach, participation, and strategy decisions. Academy of Management Review
aliases: Lobbying expenditures; Lobbying intensity

name: Campaign contributions
definition: Financial contributions that a firm, typically through its political action committee, makes to candidates and parties in order to gain access to and influence over policymakers.
sign_convention: higher values mean more campaign contributions
citations: Hillman, A. J.; Hitt, M. A. (1999). Corporate political strategy formulation: A model of approach, participation, and strategy decisions. Academy of Management Review
aliases: PAC contributions; Political action committee contributions; Political donations

name: Congressional testimony
definition: A firm's appearances before legislative bodies to provide testimony in hearings, a form of direct information provision to policymakers.
sign_convention: higher values mean more testimony appearances
aliases: Congressional hearing appearances; Legislative testimony; Witness status

name: Political connections
definition: Ties between a firm and the state, established through executives, directors or owners who hold or held government or party positions or who maintain personal relationships with government officials.
sign_convention: higher values mean stronger or more extensive political connections
citations: Faccio, M. (2006). Politically connected firms. American Economic Review; Peng, M. W.; Luo, Y. (2000). Managerial ties and firm performance in a transition economy: The nature of a micro-macro link. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Political ties; Political connection; Interlocking political ties; Government ties; Political networking; Government guanxi; Political embeddedness; Corporate political connections; CEO political connection; Managerial political ties

name: Political board ties
definition: Political connections held through a firm's board of directors, that is, directors who hold or held positions in government, legislatures or political parties.
sign_convention: higher values mean more politically connected directors on the board
aliases: Board political connections; Political connections of boards; Politically connected directors

name: Political connection loss
definition: The severance of a firm's ties to politicians or officials, for example when connected executives or directors depart or when patrons are removed from office.
sign_convention: higher values mean more (or more likely) loss of political connections
aliases: Removal of existing political connections; Political tie dissolution

name: Government dependence
definition: The extent to which a firm's operations rely on resources, contracts and support provided by the government.
sign_convention: higher values mean greater firm dependence on government resources
citations: Pfeffer, J.; Salancik, G. R. (1978). The External Control of Organizations: A Resource Dependence Perspective. Harper and Row (book)
aliases: Government contract reliance; Government-contract intensity; Resource dependence on government; Government procurement contracts; Dependence on government

name: Whistleblowing
definition: The disclosure by current or former organizational members of illegal, immoral or illegitimate practices under the control of their employer to persons or organizations able to take action.
sign_convention: higher values mean whistleblowing occurred (or is more likely)
citations: Near, J. P.; Miceli, M. P. (1985). Organizational dissidence: The case of whistle-blowing. Journal of Business Ethics
aliases: Whistle blowing; Whistle-blowing

name: Corporate litigation
definition: Formal legal disputes in which a firm sues or is sued, used as an outcome or as a form of conflict between organizations.
sign_convention: higher values mean more (or more likely) litigation involving the firm
aliases: Lawsuits; Litigation; Legal disputes; Likelihood of litigation; Probability of litigation

name: Patent litigation
definition: Legal action in which a patent owner sues another party for patent infringement, or the likelihood of such a suit between two firms.
sign_convention: higher values mean more (or more likely) patent infringement litigation between the parties
citations: Somaya, D. (2012). Patent strategy and management: An integrative review and research agenda. Journal of Management
aliases: Patent infringement suit; Patent lawsuit; Patent infringement litigation

name: Institutionalization
definition: The degree to which rules, norms and practices have become established, embedded and taken for granted within an organization, relationship or institutional environment.
sign_convention: higher values mean rules and norms are more firmly established and embedded
citations: Tolbert, P. S.; Zucker, L. G. (1983). Institutional sources of change in the formal structure of organizations: The diffusion of civil service reform, 1880-1935. Administrative Science Quarterly
aliases: Institutionalization of norms; Degree of institutionalization

name: Institutional embeddedness
definition: The degree to which an organization or actor is embedded within the dominant institutional field or macroculture of its environment, reflected in low awareness of, openness to and motivation for alternatives.
sign_convention: higher values mean the actor is more embedded in the dominant institutional arrangements
citations: Greenwood, R.; Suddaby, R. (2006). Institutional entrepreneurship in mature fields: The Big Five accounting firms. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Field embeddedness; Embeddedness in institutional field

name: Political ideology
definition: The core beliefs about how society and authority should be structured, ranging from liberal to conservative, that characterize a collective political actor or setting such as a government, legislature, regulator, party or industry. The ideology of an individual person, of a single organization's members or of a local community has its own entries.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more conservative ideology
citations: Chin, M. K.; Hambrick, D. C.; Trevino, L. K. (2013). Political ideologies of CEOs: The influence of executives' values on corporate social responsibility. Administrative Science Quarterly
aliases: Liberal-conservative orientation; Political conservatism; Partisanship

name: Trade association membership
definition: A firm's membership in an industry trade association, which often entails participation in the association's collective political action and self-regulation programs.
sign_convention: higher values mean the firm is a member of the trade association
citations: King, A. A.; Lenox, M. J. (2000). Industry self-regulation without sanctions: The chemical industry's Responsible Care program. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Industry association membership; Participation in industry self-regulation; Self-regulation program participation

name: Shareholder protection
definition: The extent to which a country's corporate and securities law defines and protects the rights of shareholders, especially minority shareholders, against expropriation by controlling insiders and managers.
sign_convention: higher values mean stronger legal protection of shareholders
citations: La Porta, R., Lopez-de-Silanes, F., Shleifer, A., & Vishny, R. W. (1998). Law and finance. Journal of Political Economy, 106(6), 1113-1155.
aliases: Investor protection; Shareholder rights protection; Minority shareholder protection; Anti-director rights; Legal protection of shareholders; Shareholder protection policy

name: Institutional equivalence
definition: The degree to which two organizations are embedded in the same set of institutional fields, in particular the same industry and the same geographic community, so that each is a salient reference point for the other's practices and evaluations.
sign_convention: higher values mean the two organizations share more of the same institutional fields
citations: Marquis, C., & Tilcsik, A. (2016). Institutional equivalence: How industry and community peers influence corporate philanthropy. Organization Science, 27(5), 1325-1341.
aliases: Institutional equivalents; Industry and community peers; Shared institutional fields; Institutionally equivalent firms

name: Corporate social performance
definition: A firm's overall configuration of principles of social responsibility, processes of social responsiveness, and observable outcomes as they relate to the firm's societal relationships. It is the umbrella for a firm's social, environmental and stakeholder-related conduct and outcomes.
sign_convention: higher values mean better social performance
citations: Wood, D. J. (1991). Corporate social performance revisited. Academy of Management Review
aliases: CSP; Social performance; Corporate responsibility performance; Corporate social responsibility performance

name: Corporate social responsibility
definition: Voluntary corporate actions, not required by law, that integrate social and environmental concerns into the firm's operations and stakeholder relations and appear to further some social good beyond the firm's interests. It captures positive engagement (strengths), whereas overall ratings that net strengths against concerns reflect Corporate social performance.
sign_convention: higher values mean more CSR activity
citations: Wood, D. J. (1991). Corporate social performance revisited. Academy of Management Review
aliases: CSR; CSR engagement; Corporate social responsibility engagement; CSR strengths; Socially responsible activities; Corporate social responsibility activities

name: Corporate philanthropy
definition: A firm's voluntary transfer of money, goods or services to charitable, community or social causes, including giving through corporate foundations and donation programs.
sign_convention: higher values mean more corporate giving
citations: Godfrey, P. C. (2005). The relationship between corporate philanthropy and shareholder wealth: A risk management perspective. Academy of Management Review
aliases: Corporate giving; Corporate charitable contributions; Corporate charitable donation; Corporate philanthropic contributions; Disaster relief giving

name: Employee-related CSR
definition: The extent to which a firm treats its employees well and invests in relations with them through practices such as health and safety, union and employee relations, human capital development and profit sharing.
sign_convention: higher values mean better treatment of and stronger relations with employees
aliases: Employee treatment; Employee relations; Attention to employees; Employment-related corporate social responsibility; Firm-employee relationship strength

name: Internal CSR
definition: Substantive, inward-looking social responsibility actions directed at the firm's internal stakeholders and operations, as opposed to visible communication aimed at external audiences.
sign_convention: higher values mean more internal CSR actions
citations: Hawn, O.; Ioannou, I. (2016). Mind the gap: The interplay between external and internal actions in the case of corporate social responsibility. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Internal CSR actions

name: External CSR
definition: Highly visible public initiatives and communication about social responsibility intended to influence external audiences and generate public endorsement of the firm.
sign_convention: higher values mean more external CSR actions
citations: Hawn, O.; Ioannou, I. (2016). Mind the gap: The interplay between external and internal actions in the case of corporate social responsibility. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: External CSR actions

name: CSR executive position
definition: Whether a firm has established a top-level executive position, such as a chief sustainability officer, whose primary responsibility is corporate sustainability or social responsibility.
sign_convention: higher values mean the firm has (adopted) a CSR executive position
aliases: Chief sustainability officer presence; Adoption of a CSR executive position; Chief sustainability officer

name: Employee participation in corporate social initiatives
definition: An individual employee's participation in a firm-sponsored program with an explicit social impact goal, such as a corporate social initiative that assigns employees to pro-social projects.
sign_convention: higher values mean the employee participated
aliases: Corporate social initiative participation; CSI participation

name: Corporate environmental management
definition: The strategies, practices and technologies through which a firm addresses the natural environmental impact of its operations, from compliance-oriented pollution control to proactive environmental initiatives.
sign_convention: higher values mean more extensive environmental management activity
aliases: Corporate environmentalism; Pro-environmental practices; Corporate environmental actions; Corporate sustainability practices; Environmental practices

name: Environmental performance
definition: A firm's or facility's realized impact on the natural environment, such as emissions, waste, resource use and pollution incidents, relative to what is expected or to its own past.
sign_convention: higher values mean better environmental performance (less environmental harm)
aliases: Environmental improvement; Environmental performance improvement; Environmental rating

name: Eco-efficiency
definition: The extent to which a firm's environmental impacts or resource intensity are minimized relative to its level of production or output.
sign_convention: higher values mean less environmental impact per unit of output
aliases: Environmental efficiency

name: Proactive environmental strategy
definition: The degree to which a firm's environmental strategy goes beyond regulatory compliance and reactive pollution control toward voluntary, anticipatory environmental management.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more proactive environmental strategy
citations: Sharma, S.; Vredenburg, H. (1998). Proactive corporate environmental strategy and the development of competitively valuable organizational capabilities. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Environmental proactivity; Environmental strategy proactiveness; Environmental strategy

name: Pollution prevention practices
definition: Operational, procedural, material or equipment changes a firm or plant adopts to reduce the generation of pollution at its source, as distinct from end-of-pipe pollution control.
sign_convention: higher values mean more pollution prevention practices adopted
citations: Klassen, R. D.; Whybark, D. C. (1999). The impact of environmental technologies on manufacturing performance. Academy of Management Journal
aliases: Pollution prevention; Pollution prevention technologies; P2 practices

name: Corporate social irresponsibility
definition: Corporate actions that violate moral or legal norms and adversely affect the legitimate claims of the firm's stakeholders.
sign_convention: higher values mean more socially irresponsible activity
citations: Strike, V. M.; Gao, J.; Bansal, P. (2006). Being good while being bad: Social responsibility and the international diversification of US firms. Journal of International Business Studies
aliases: CSI; Social irresponsibility; Socially irresponsible activities; CSR concerns

name: Corporate misconduct
definition: Organizational behavior that transgresses legal, ethical or professional norms and is judged as wrongdoing by a social control agent, such as regulatory enforcement actions, fraud or corruption.
sign_convention: higher values mean more misconduct
aliases: Organizational misconduct; Corporate illegality; Corporate wrongdoing; Organizational wrongdoing; Illegal corporate behavior; Corporate crime

name: Financial misconduct
definition: Clear, egregious and material violations of accounting or securities rules, typically observed through financial restatements or securities enforcement actions.
sign_convention: higher values mean financial misconduct occurred or is more extensive
aliases: Financial misrepresentation; Financial restatement; Accounting fraud; Securities fraud; Securities violation; Securities enforcement action; Financial fraud

name: Violation severity
definition: The seriousness of a corporate legal or ethical violation, reflecting its duration, magnitude of harm and the sanctions it attracts.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more serious violation
aliases: Seriousness of illegality; Misconduct severity

name: Negative organizational events
definition: Discrete adverse occurrences attributed to an organization, such as accidents, product recalls or scandals, considered as events that expose it to stakeholder blame and reputational damage. The accumulated stock of such events treated as a source of organizational learning is Failure experience.
sign_convention: higher values mean more or more serious negative events
aliases: Negative event; Adverse organizational event; Organizational crisis

name: Event controllability
definition: The degree to which a negative event could have been prevented or controlled by the focal organization, and is therefore attributable to it.
sign_convention: higher values mean the event was more controllable by (attributable to) the firm
aliases: Attribution of responsibility for an adverse event

name: Stakeholder relations
definition: The nature and quality of a firm's relationships with the groups and individuals who can affect or are affected by the achievement of its purpose, including how it prioritizes, manages and engages them and how they respond.
sign_convention: higher values mean stronger, more cooperative stakeholder relations
aliases: Stakeholder relationships; Stakeholder capital

name: Stakeholder orientation
definition: The degree of attention and priority a firm gives to nonfinancial stakeholders such as employees, customers, suppliers and communities, relative to shareholders.
sign_convention: higher values mean greater attention to nonfinancial stakeholders
aliases: Attention to stakeholders; Corporate attention to stakeholders

name: Stakeholder management
definition: The extent to which a firm actively manages and invests in its relationships with primary stakeholders who have contributed capital or bear risk in the firm, beyond its own needs and legal requirements.
sign_convention: higher values mean more extensive stakeholder management
citations: Hillman, A. J.; Keim, G. D. (2001). Shareholder value, stakeholder management, and social issues: What's the bottom line?. Strategic Management Journal
aliases: Stakeholder investment; Investment in stakeholders; Primary stakeholder management

name: Stakeholder engagement
definition: The degree to which a firm maintains formal processes for consulting, involving and communicating with its stakeholders on the basis of mutual trust and cooperation.
sign_convention: higher values mean more stakeholder engagement
aliases: Stakeholder dialogue

name: Stakeholder support
definition: The degree of cooperation rather than conflict that a firm receives from its stakeholders, including their willingness to endorse, contribute to or continue supporting the organization.
sign_convention: higher values mean more stakeholder cooperation and support
aliases: Stakeholder cooperation; Stakeholder conflict (reverse); Stakeholder endorsement

name: Stakeholder pressure
definition: Demands, expectations and challenges directed at a firm by external stakeholders, such as communities, activists, regulators and customers, to change its social or environmental conduct.
sign_convention: higher values mean more stakeholder pressure on the firm
aliases: Stakeholder pressures; Social pressure; External pressure for social responsibility

name: Social movement contention
definition: Confrontational tactics such as boycotts, protests and lawsuits used by activists or social movement organizations to directly challenge a corporation.
sign_convention: higher values mean more contentious challenges against the firm
citations: King, B. G. (2008). A political mediation model of corporate response to social movement activism. Administrative Science Quarterly
aliases: Contentious private politics; Activist challenges; Social movement activism against firms; Private politics

name: Boycott targeting
definition: Whether a firm has been targeted by an activist-organized boycott, a contentious tactic that publicly vilifies the firm to pressure it into changing its practices.
sign_convention: higher values mean the firm was boycotted
citations: King, B. G. (2008). A political mediation model of corporate response to social movement activism. Administrative Science Quarterly
aliases: Social activist boycott; Boycott; Being boycotted

name: Social issue salience
definition: The pervasiveness and intensity of stakeholder concern about a social issue, reflecting how many stakeholders care about it and how strongly.
sign_convention: higher values mean the issue is more salient
aliases: Issue salience; Issue attention

name: Stakeholder salience
definition: The importance that managers attribute to particular stakeholder groups, reflecting the perceived power, legitimacy and urgency of their claims on the organization.
sign_convention: higher values mean the stakeholder group is perceived as more important
citations: Mitchell, R. K.; Agle, B. R.; Wood, D. J. (1997). Toward a theory of stakeholder identification and salience: Defining the principle of who and what really counts. Academy of Management Review
aliases: Perceived stakeholder importance; Perceived importance of organizational stakeholders; Primary stakeholder importance

name: Local community characteristics
definition: Socioeconomic, political and attitudinal attributes of the geographic community in which a firm or facility operates that shape the demands it faces from local stakeholders.
sign_convention: higher values mean the characteristic is more pronounced
aliases: Community characteristics; Local community context

name: Community environmental preferences
definition: The strength of a local population's interest in and demand for environmental quality, as revealed by its environmental group membership or voting.
sign_convention: higher values mean stronger community environmental preferences
aliases: Environmental sensitivity; Community environmental activism; Demand for environmental quality

name: Community political ideology
definition: The prevailing sociopolitical values of a community on the conservative-liberal spectrum, typically captured by electoral outcomes.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more conservative community
aliases: Local political ideology; Community conservatism; Community liberalism (reverse)

name: Community income
definition: The income level of the population in the community where a firm or facility is located, used as an indicator of the community's resources and its capacity to press claims on the firm.
sign_convention: higher values mean a wealthier community
aliases: Community wealth; Local median household income; Per capita income of the community

name: Audience receptivity
definition: The extent to which an audience or community is predisposed to engage with and support a given message, cause or offering because of its values, education or resources.
sign_convention: higher values mean a more receptive audience
aliases: Audience receptiveness; Values alignment of the audience

name: Customer satisfaction
definition: The aggregate evaluation by a firm's own customers of their overall experience with its products or services, as captured in satisfaction surveys or indices. Public ratings and reviews of a product or work by consumers or critics are Audience quality evaluation.
sign_convention: higher values mean more satisfied customers
aliases: Customer satisfaction score

name: Voluntary disclosure
definition: A firm's discretionary release of information about its prospects and performance to investors and other external audiences, such as management earnings forecasts.
sign_convention: higher values mean more extensive, earlier or more forward-looking voluntary disclosure
aliases: Management earnings forecasts; Management guidance; Discretionary disclosure; Forecast horizon

name: Loan contract terms
definition: The terms and structure of a firm's bank loans, such as loan type, stated purpose, pricing and the distribution of the loan across the lending syndicate.
sign_convention: higher values mean more of the named loan attribute
